speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I had a report made to me in regard to this matter by the Minister of Labour. The situation is a very simple one. A board of conciliation was appointed, and the law provides that until a report has been made and filed by the board no strike or lockout shall take place. While the board was carrying on its investigations, the men went out on strike. The
Minister of Labour reached the conclusion that to proceed with the Board of Conciliation under those circumstances was not consistent with due respect to the law of this country, and he therefore directed the board to delay any further investigation until the men had returned to their duty and obeyed the law.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Committee on the following proposed resolutions; Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide,-
1.	That the powers, jurisdiction and authority of the Commissioner and Controller of Paper should be confirmed and extended to such extent as may be necessary to enable him to fully complete all work and investigations begun 'by him prior to the declaration of peace, under the provisions of the Orders in Council relating to such investigations, and to determine all questions and to make all necessary orders with respect to matters begun by or coming before him prior to the declaration of peace.
2.	That the powers, jurisdiction and authority of the Paper Control Tribunal under the Order in Council of September 16, 1918, (P.C. 2270), should be confirmed and extended as may be necessary to enable said Paper Control Tribunal to finally determine after the declaration of peace all matters pending before and not finally determined by it upon the date of such declaration ; and that the powers, jurisdiction and authority of the said Tribunal should be further extended to such extent as may be necessary to enable it to hear and finally determine all matters and questions brought before it subsequent to the declaration of peace on appeal from any act done by or order or decision of the Commissioner and Controller under the provisions of the foregoing resolution.
3.	That except for the purpose of finally completing all matters undertaken and determining all questions arising prior to the declaration of peace, the powers, authority and jurisdiction of the said Commissioner and Controller of Paper of the said Paper Control Tribunal shall cease upon the declaration of peace.
Sir THOMAiS WHITE:	The object
of these resolutions, and of the legislation which will be founded upon them, is to enable the Commissioner and Controller of Paper to complete, to the extent' that is necessary after the declaration of peace, the work and investigations begun by him under the Orders in Council under which he has been acting. Let me describe the present situation. The Commissioner and Controller of Newsprint Paper has, in pursuance of the powers conferred upon him, made orders respecting the price which is to be paid by publishers in . Canada for newsprint paper from July 1st of last year. Those orders of the commissioner are at present in appeal before what is called the Paper Control Tribunal, consisting of three judges appointed for the purpose of reviewing the findings of the Commissioner and Controller of Newsprint Paper. Some little time ago

Probably my hon. friend is not as familiar with the situation as I had assumed, and I do' not wonder at it. There is at present a Commissioner

and Controller of Newsprint Paper whose duties are to make investigations from time to time and fix the prices to be paid by Canadian publishers to the manufacturers of newsprint paper, and to enforce his orders so that newsprint will be distributed according to the requirements of the Canadian press. It is also his duty to make orders, whereby the manufacturers of newsprint paper who supply less than their proportion of the newsprint paper required by Canadian publishers shall pay to those manufacturers who furnish more than their proportionate share, what is called the differential. That administration has been going on for two years, and the commissioner and controjler (Mr. R. A. Pringle, K.C.), has made many orders fixing prices, and also with respect to the payment of the differential.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext: At whose request was he appointed, and by whom was the appointment made?

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
The Dominion Government appointed him upon representations made that if the price of newsprint paper was not regulated, many newspapers in Canada would have to cease publication. Now, answering more particularly the question of the leader of the Opposition, dissatisfaction having been expressed by the newspaper publishers and the newsprint manufacturers as well, as to the orders made. by the Commissioner and Controller of Newsprint Paper with respect to prices, and with respect to the amount of differential which should be paid by some manufacturers to others, the Government created an Appeal Tribunal consisting of: Mr. Justice Middleton of Ontario, Mr. Justice Archer of Quebec, and Mr. Justice White of New Brunswick. The proceedings before the commissioner and controller, upon which his findings as to prices and as to the differential were based, are now before that Appeal Tribunal for review and judgment. It may be some time before their decision is rendered, and even after it is rendered

there will be matters of accounting which will take a considerable time to adjust. In addition to that, it is necessary to continue the powers of the Controller after the declaration of peace, in order that he may enforce his decisions, and the final decision of the Appeal Tribunal. In other words, unless this legislation is passed, jt is quite probable that the orders of the Controller of Newsprint Paper, and the decisions thereon of the Appeal Tribunal, will become null and void, and not susceptible of enforcement without retroactive legislation at a subsequent session of Parliament.
Let me point out the last provision of the resolution:
That except for the purpose of finally completing- all matters undertaken and determining all questions arising prior to the declaration of peace, the powers, authority and jurisdiction of the said Commissioner and Controller of Paper of the said Paper Control Tribunal cease upon the declaration of peace.
That is to say, the powers which we have given to him come to an end upon the declaration of peace subject to the carrying into effect of orders already made and the completion of work undertaken will be authorized by this legislation we are now asking Parliament to pass.

speechtext: The British Empire at present is at war with four powers -Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria and Turkey. Preliminary peace has been signed with Germany, but officially and technically we are still at war with her. Before peace is an accomplished fact, and before a proclamation can be made that a state of peace exists among all the belligerent nations, it will be necessary that the peace treaties with the several powers with whom Great Britain and her allies have been at war, shall be ratified and approved by the several legislatures concerned. The Prime Minister made a comprehensive statement with respect to that the other day. While we do not know how long that will be, it may well be a couple of months. This legislation is absolutely necessary unless all the proceedings of the Newsprint Commissioner and Controller, and of the Appeal Tribunal, are to be nullified through lapse of their powers by reason of the expiration of the war.

The commercial interests of the country are very much interested in 'this matter, and, if the Paper Control Tribunal have no such authority, I would like to know why it is that the Government have shown so much consideration for the interests of the newspaper?

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext: The action taken was by virtue of the jurisdiction of the Government under the War Measures Act. It was a war measure. The press of this country is not precisely in the same position as private enterprise. I think that no one in this House will seriously contend that it is. It has a private aspect, because the newspapers are privately owned, just as other businesses are owned; but, on the other hand, the press has a public aspect not possessed by any other business of which I am aware. That is especially so in time of war. It is vital in the public interest that at such time the newspapers of the country should disseminate information as to the war,-information from the front, and information on important measures undertaken by Government in connection with the prosecution of the war. Further than that, and even more important, the press renders a national service of the highest possible value in encouraging and inspiring the people to continue effort until the war is won,-and in tkat and other respects no press in the world has done more valuable service than has the press of the Dominion. It was not only a question of keeping the public informed as to the progress of the war by land and sea, but of encouraging the people and urging them to greater effort - maintaining that spirit which is so necessary for " carrying on" until victory is accomplished. Having regard to those" two aspects, I cannot imagine any greater calamity to the people of this country, short of something that would cause acute physical distress and suffering, than that the press of Canada, or any considerable part of it, should have been forced to close down. When the war broke out supplies of pulp which had been available from northern Europe to this continent were shut off, and the result was that the supply of newsprint paper was without that competition.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
How much pulp from
northern Europe or anywhere else is imported into Canada?

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext: I am speaking of the North American continent.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext: The hon. minister is talking of Canada.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
I am speaking of the North American continent, (because as a matter of fact the question cannot be intelligently discussed unless the requirements of both the United States and Canada are taken into account. An abnormal situation arose under which it was possible for the manufacturers of newsprint papier to make very large profits by reason of the prices which they were enabled to get in Canada and in the United States. By reason of that same war condition the newspapers were put in a position where they were threatened with extinction. I do not say that all of them would have had to cease publication, but I have not the slightest doubt that many of them would have been obliged to do so, with great resultant loss to the Canadian public. In those circumstances the Government had not the slightest hesitation in intervening early in the war and fixing a price which enabled the press of Canada to continue their operations and to supply the publicity which was so necessary, as I pointed out, in connection with the war.
Now, so far as I know nobody has been hurt. I have looked carefully over the balance sheets of the newsprint manufacturers of this country, and on the whole they have done very well. I am glad they have. 1 have no criticism whatever tp make of our newsprint manufacturers in connection with the conduct, of their business. I do not allege that there is any combine or anything irregular at all, but by reason of the conditions that arose-the demand from the United States, the demand from Canada, and the limitation upon supply, they were able to make very large profits; whereas the newspapers were in a position, as I said, where they were likely to be obliged to close up.
Under the circumstances, and in the national interest as a war measure, the Government fixed the price of newsprint. Representations having been made on behalf of the manufacturers of newsprint paper that the price was too low, the Dominion Government appointed a commissioner and controller of newsprint paper. His duties were to make appropriate inquiry and investigation into the conditions governing the manufacture of newsprint paper, as to price, and as to distribution. He has carried out his exceedingly onerous and difficult duties over a period of two years with great credit to himself and with fairness to all concerned. We have had a 
considerable amount of trouble in connection with this matter, but it was war time, and trouble cannot be avoided by governments in war time. The fact that there is difficulty in dealing with a situation is no good reason why it should not be dealt with, if it can be dealt with, if the public interest so requires. We were able to deal with the newsprint situation because it is a comparatively simple business. There are not many engaged in the manufacture of newsprint; the business is carried on comparatively simply by distribution to the newspapers of Canada and by shipment to the United States. The entire amount of newsprint paper used in Canada is only about II per cent of the entire production of Canadian mills; the balance goes to the United States. The newsprint industry is one of very great value to Canada by reason of the fact that its exportable surplus materially assists our international trade balance and brings a good deal of wealth into the country. But so far as I am concerned that latter question does not arise. Because questions have been put forward, more especially because they have been put forward before in the House, and because there was some criticism of the course of the Government in fixing the price, I have thought it advisable to give this general explanation.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
I appreciate the extensive explanation the minister has given in reply to my inquiry. I note, however, that he admits that newspapers are commercial enterprises just as other commercial industries in this country are, and I submit that while we are willing to agree with him in regard to the assistance and encouragement that the press should receive at the hands of the Government, we say that there is no just reason for discrimination as between commercial enterprises of various kinds. There has been a good deal of criticism of the commercial interests of this country in regard to the high cost of living.. The cost of wrapping paper may, in the estimation of the Government, be only a trifling affair so far as the high cost of living is concerned, but it is one of the items that bears upon that question. Wrapping paper costs to-day three times as much as it cost in 1914, yet the Government, through the Paper Cbntrol Tribunal, has taken no notice of that aspect of the matter. The commercial interests of this country during the last four years have realized that while the Government are prepared to protect the newspapers so far'as their supply of paper is concerned, they have taken no interest in the requirements of the commercial in.

terests, the large wholesale and retail concerns, so far as wrapping paper, which they use extensively, is concerned. That neglect has tended to increase the high cost of living, because all these little details go to increase the cost of delivering the manufactured article to the consumer. The newspapers are pretty well able to take care of themselves; although the price of newsprint paper has been arranged for them by the Government, they have increased the price of the newspaper to the purchaser by 100 per cent during the last four years.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
I am always delighted to hear the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White), especially when he is defending some proposition which in his heart and mind as an economist he knows is unsound, because then he rises to real heights of eloquence. His defence of the press of Canada this morning and his remarks about the usefulness of the press to the country would almost make one think that at one time he had been associated with that department of life. I objected yesterday to the Government paying money to the press, directly or indirectly; to subsidizing the press in any way out of the public money, because that is an unwholesome condition and is liable to vitiate the springs of public information. What does the minister say to-day? He says that although the war is over he proposes to continue a system whereby, at the expense of an important commercial interest, the papers shall get their-the minister shakes his head, but I think I am right -the papers shall get their newsprint at a price lower than they would have to pay if they had to go into the open market and buy it. There is no other reason for the control of the price. The control of price is not to make the newspapers pay more for their newsprint; it is in order that they shall pay less than the commercial rate. The minister saidi that newspapers would have gone out of business during the war had the Government not made this order. What does that mean? It means that the very life and death of the newspapers depended upon the Government's action. Is that a wholesome condidtion of affairs? The minister knows that it is not. No newspaper , should be dependent for its existence upon an order given by the Government that they should get their raw materials at less than a fair price. The war is now over; at least the fighting is done. Let us get out of the state of mind of the person who is running to a fire; let us get down again to a sound economic basis. Let the newspapers pay what they
should pay for their paper; do not order the people who manufacture paper to sell their product to one set of customers at a lower price than that at which they sell it to other customers. If the manufacturers of newsprint are making a great deal of money and are sending out of the country a great deal of paper-which is a very good thing, because it tends to make our exchange situation less unfavourable-then let the minister take a proper share of their excess profits, but do not cause the money which should go into the public coffers not to be collected simply because the paper manufacturers have to give to certain newspapers or to all the newspapers their raw material at lower than the cost price.

speechtext: If any one has specially suffered during the last few years it is the newspaper industry. I could name a score of newspapers in Ontario that have had to go out of business. In cities like St. Thomas, Stratford, Chatham and Windsor, where there were formerly two papers, most of the Liberal papers have gone out of business because they could not continue under the existing conditions, and unfortunately the Liberal party is not properly represented through the press in those communities. That is due very largely to the excessive cost of newsprint, and if any steps are going to be taken to limit profiteering, a good start will be made by dealing with the newsprint mills. Under conditions that exist on this continent they can get a larger price in the United States than in Canada owing partly to the fact that the United States has practically worked out its pulp-wood area, and partly to the fact that it is exporting a large part of its product to South America.

speechtext:
Because the United
States supply of pulpwood has been practically worked out the newsprint mills are able to form a combine to-day, perhaps with a greater efficiency than any other industry that exists in Canada. The evidence shows that there is one selling organization for practically every newsprint mill in the Dominion, and with a condition of that kind they can boost the price to anything they like. Therefore, if there is one industry that should be under some kind of government control, it is the newsprint industry. That is sound reasoning from the standpoint of those who are against profiteering and combines, from (the point of view that it is desirable that the newspapers of this country should be cheap, and that the proprietors should be in a position to publish good newspapers and give good news to the people of Canada.

speechtext: Or, if my understanding is right, is it not at the request of the newspapermen that the Government decided to regulate the price of paper, and then appointed Mr. Pringle to investigate the matter in order to see on what basis a regulation of the prices ought to be made? Mr. Pringle investigated; he made certain rules and orders; those rules and orders were appealed from. Of course, during that time they were suspended, if I understand rightly, and things have been going on as usual. What the minister wants is that, during the time of war, the paper manufacturers shall be subject to those rules and orders made by Mr. Pringle, if they are confirmed by the Appeal Tribunal, and that, at the cessation of hostilities or when peace comes, those rules and orders shall cease to have effect. subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
Not quite. My hon. driend is right up to his last sentence. speechtext:
I want . to say a
few words in reply to the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) who claimed that the Government was controlling the price of paper especially for the interest of the newspapers. As a matter of fact, my hon. friend and the House will probably be surprised to know that two or two and one-half years ago there existed a large combine and trust which controlled the pulp and paper industry on this continent. I want to point out further that action was brought in the United States by the Federal Commission to put an end to this trust and combine to control prices, and the members -there were some five or six of them and several were Canadians, pleaded guilty of having a trust and combine and were each fined $2,500.
As a result of that combination the price of newsprint was enormously enhanced; in
fact, the intervention of the Government was due in a measure to the fact that this combination existed, but notwithstanding the effort to control the price of paper, it has been increased almost double in this country. The result was that the newspapers were obliged to raise the price of their newspapers to the subscriber, and the extra cost to the subscribers in the Dominion has been in the neighbourhood of millions.
I have not the figures with me at the moment, but during the last two years since this Government began to control the paper situation the manufacturers of newsprint have made enormous revenues and have paid very much larger dividends, ranging from 8 to 20 per cent. A large portion of those dividends was paid on pure water. The capitalization of one company, for instance, has been doubled and the dividends were paid on pure water. Another fact I wish to emphasize is that since the Government took control of the situation the value of the stock on pulp and paper companies in Canada has been increased by some $9,900,000 or $10,000,000. That is not all due to the fact that they have sold paper to the newspaper publishers of Canada, because, as the Minister of'Finance has pointed out, only eleven per cent of the product of our pulp and paper mills is sold in this country, the other 89 per cent going to the United States. Of course, we are not particularly interested in the price that they pay, but I do not suppose it is desirable or neighbourly that they should be expected to pay too. high a price. But that has nothing to do with the object of the resolution. That stands on its merits, and I have merely made these remarks in reply to what has been said to the effect that in instituting this paper control an effort was made to control not only the newspapers, but' all their subscribers throughout the country.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
I wish to correct a few misstatements that have been made. Prior to the war many of the largest manufacturers on this continent, the International Paper Company, for instance, had not paid a dividend on their preferred stock for years, and the result was that the accumulation of unpaid interest on their preferred stock was almost equal to their preferred capital. Prior to the war the normal price of paper was around two cents, but when the war broke out the price of paper and everything else went up. Immediately the publishers of Canada came to' the Govern-



ment and represented, as the Minister of Finance has told us, that unless the price of paper was controlled, the publishers would have to go out of business. I do not wish to accuse the Minister of Finance of making a statement that was not correct but I think he must have get those representations a little twisted. I think the publishers told the Government that if the price was not controlled it would be the Government that would have to go out of business. That evidently had an effect upon the Government, and practically without giving the manufacturers any opportunity of being heard the Minister of Finance fixed the price of newsprint a't $50 a ton-an advance of 25 per cent above the normal price. At the normal price of two cents a pound it was only those manufacturers who had well equipped plants, well located with regard to cheap power and cheap labour, who could pay any dividends. The manufacturers objected to the price b^ing fixed, and after very lengthy discussions with the Government they succeeded in getting a commissioner, Mr. Pringle, appointed to investigate the cost of paper, and his finding was that the average cost of making paper was $57.50 a ton! We were therefore forced by the Government to sell paper to the whole press of Canada at $50 a ton, or $7.50 below cost. The manufacturers continued to make representations and fight for the right of doing business in this free country and at last the commissioner made another ruling, approved by Order in Council, whereby the price of newsprint was fixed for a further period at $58. At that time it was costing $57 to make it.

It is said that the press of Canada would have had to go out of business if the price of paper had not been fixed. I should like to know what branch of industry there is in Canada or any other country which has better facilities for putting before the public the reasons why they have to charge an increased price for their product. It was a very simple thing for the newspapers to tell their patrons why the cost of advertising space had to be increased and why the price of newspaper had to be raised to the subscriber. After the price of paper was fixed, did the newspapers continue to charge the same for their advertising space? No, they increased their rates. I believe that many newspaper publishers in this country within the last two years have

made a great deal more money and paid much higher dividends, or were in a position to pay them, than many of our manufacturers, but we do not hear anything about that.
After Mr. Pringle had been appointed commissioner he asked the Government for permission to investigate not only the cost of making paper but the publishing end as well because the manufacturers insisted that if they were going to be held to account and have their business investigated and the price of paper fixed it was only fair that an inquiry should be made into what the publishers of this country were making. Mr. Pringle was given power to investigate the publishers. , A committee of four members of the Government was also appointed to consider the situation, and I understand that Mr. Pringle in discussing the situation at one time with one of the members of that committee intimated that he would probably have to investigate the publishers to see whether they were making or losing money.
That gentleman told Mr. Pringle to keep his hands off the publishers and conduct no investigation in regard to them. This was verbal, but so as to put the matter beyond any possibility of mistake he went to his office and wrote him a letter forbidding him to hold any inquiry as to what the publishers were doing. He could investigate the manufacturers' affairs, but he must not put his hands on the publishers.

I am glad to hear that this measure which is now before the House is intended .at some time to put an end. to this vicious and vile method of fixing the prices of an article, below cost of production at least. Only on two articles that I know anything about were prices fixed- wheat and paper. The price of wheat was fixed at $2.21 a bushel, which is at least one hundred and twenty per cent over normal. I have no objection to that, and I am not jealous about it. But the same Government fixed the price of paper at only t.wenty-five per cent over normal in. war time when the cost of production went up

one hundred per cent. The member for 'Springfield and the member for Toronto (Mr. Hocken) made allusion to the high cost of paper, which has nearly doubled. .Are you surprised at that? Are you aware that the price of pulp wood has at least doubled what it was in 1914 and prior to that? Are you aware that many other things that go into the construction of paper, for instance, Fourdrinier wire, which is one of the big items, have advanced enormously? We figured the matter, taking eighteen months prior to the war, and -wo find that the cost of this wire previous to 1914 was $212 a piece and the life of it *was almost six weeks,- but since that time the average cost of the same wire has been $490 and the average life less than three weeks. That means that it is more than double the price with less than half the life, and that is only one example out of many.
I am not surprised. The machine tenders prior to the war were only paid fifty-five cents an hour. To-day we are paying $1.35 to the same men and on an eight-hour shift. Not only that, but when one of these wires I spoke of breaks, that means calling out the whole force to make repairs, and it takes them three hours to change that wire and put on a new one. During that tune the whole plant is shut down. That occurs about once in three weeks, whereas it only used to happen once in six weeks. That adds to the cost. Furthermore, if the men we call out are engaged on that wire for two hours, we have to pay them for a six-hour period at $1.35 per hour as compared with the former rate of fifty-five cents and a payment simply for the actual time they were at work-that is if they were working for four hours, or three hours, we paid them simply for the actual time they worked. Do not be surprised, therefore, if you have to pay more for your paper than you formerly did, or if you are called upon to pay twice the price you paid in normal times, because the cost of making paper is twice the amount it was prior to the war.

speechtext:
Two or three [DOT]statements have been made by my hon. friend (Mr. McCrea) which I feel I must deal with. In the first place, he intimates that the Government at the beginning acted in a very hurried manner with respect to this question.
Mr. MeCREA: The Government acted quickly, and without proper information.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
Let us see how quickly we did act. It was brought to my attention by the press that on account of the rising price of newsprint some newspapers in the country would probably have to close up. I at once convened a meeting of representatives of the newsprint paper manufacturers and of the press of Canada in my office, and talked to the representatives of both interests. The matter was very fully discussed, and I asked them to appoint a small committee on either side for the purpose of getting together in conference and seeing if they couM not reach a conclusion which would be fair to both parties concerned. They had more than one meeting, but failed to agree. I associated with this conference of the joint committees an official from my office, Mr. Breadner, who was very familiar with matters relating to the newsprint and other industries in this country. I say to my hon. friend that for a period of five weeks we laboured absolutely fruitlessly trying to bring the newsprint manufacturers and the newspaper publishers to a fair agreement respecting the matter of price. Think of it, five weeks.
Mr. iMcCREA:	You insisted, or rather
you wrote a letter, did you not, to Mr. Chahoon to the effect that if we did not agree on $2.60 you were going to fix that as the price. Are you surprised that the manufacturers would not agree to a price which was proven to be less than cost?

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
I do not recall
what I wrote to Mr. Chahoon, but I doubt very nfuch if I mentioned the price. What I did say to those people was: If you cannot agree, as the representatives of all the other industries that I called together during the war have agreed, I shall fix the price. I say the Government was right in doing that. If a situation arises in war time that calls for attention and if every effort that is made to try and gjet the parties together is fruitless, then I maintain the Government is justified in saying to them:	If you do not get together, we are
going to act.

speechtext: Does the minister remember a conversation I had with him one day when I told him, that a couple of paper men in this country would' accept $60 per ton if he would agree to it? His answer to me was that if the paper manufacturers did not want to accept ithe price of $50 per ton, he could not do otherwise than take over the mills.

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
I do not recall
the conversation, and I think it is very much to be deprecated that a conversation between members of this House should be mentioned afterwards as conclusive evidence as to what was in intention. We came to the conclusion after an investigation carried out by my department-not by calling witnesses, but an investigation which was carried out along what would be called ordinary business lines by Mr. Breadner-that $50 was a fair price; I am speaking of the situation early in 1917. Why the price of paper before the war had only been $1.90, which is $38 a ton. We came to the conclusion that the war wms threatening-and I use the word advisedly-to make the manufacturers of newsprint rich, which is not always an unmixed advantage, and was threatening to destroy the press of Canada. The result of it was I asked Mr. Breadner when we failed to get the parties to come together, to advise me as to what was a reasonable price for newsprint paper, having regard to the increase that had taken place in the price of raw materials and of labour, and we came to the conclusion that $2.50, or $50 a ton, was a fair price	at	that time,	and that was
the amount fixed. We did not fix the price precipitately, we fixed it after we had failed to get all the parties to come together. I have been in business many years, and have had a great deal to do with affairs in many lines of industry, and I say that a more unwise thing was never done by manufacturers in any branch of industry in this country, than was done toy the manufacturers of newsprint paper when they refused to compromise with the newspaper men at that time. Had they done so, all this trouble that we have had would have been avoided. You cannot in time of war look at this thing from a hard and fast business standpoint. If a war comes along-for which, of course, the newsprint manufacturers, or the press, are not responsible-and as a result of that war one set of men are going to become millionaires, and the other set of men, or some of them, are going to be put out of business, is there not room for a fair agreement? That is the way to look at it and that is the way it should be viewed at any time. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCrea) says the publishers came down here and put a pistol to the head of the Minister of Finance. Gentlemen, there is not enough in the public life of this country to permit me to tolerate any intimidation from the newspapers or any other interests in this
country-it is not good enough. The man. does not live who can intimidate me in. the discharge of my duty and nobody has ever attempted so to interfere. If a per- ' son attempted it once, he would not attempt it again-make no mistake about that. Then what did we do? After fixing the;, price, as I say, at $50 a ton, representations were made that the prices of raw material and labour were still going up, and we said: "We will appoint a Commissioner and Controller of Newsprint who will make a judicial inquiry, and call for evidence and hear the interested parties, and determine what is a fair price." Who can complain if a fair price is fixed? Nobody wants, or should want, more than a fair price, and it was the duty of the commissioner and controller to fix that fair price, and after hearing all the evidence he fixed what he regarded as a fair price. My hon. friend has said that the prices of raw material and of labour have gone up. So they have, but those facts were taken into consideration by the Commissioner and Controller ' of Newsprint in the price which he fixed. The price before the war was $1.90, or $38 a ton. He fixed a price of $68 a ton and for the West $70 a ton.

Now, about a week ago I saw in the Montreal Gazette two statements-one the financial statement of the Laurentide Pulp and Paper Company, and a beautiful statement it was, and right alongside of it a diatribe against this Government by the manager and director of that company, Mr. Chahoon, as to the injustice of our action in fixing the price of newsprint paper, and the damage that had consequently been done to his shareholders. Right in the parallel column, in the first statement to which I have alluded, was a most beautiful comparison of profits-I use the word "beautiful" from the standpoint of the shareholders of the Laurentide Pulp and paper Company- showing that up to 1914 the company had made eight or nine hundred thousand dollars, and that during the subsequent years their profits had been about $1,800,000. Who was hurt in this matter? Was the Laurentide Pulp and Paper Company hurt very much?
Mr. MoCREA: Is the minister aware that part of the revenue derived by the Lauren-

tide Pulp and Paper Company comes from .its water-jx>wer and sulphide mill, which had no fixed price on its product?

subtopic: POWERS, JURISDICTION, AND AUTHORITY OP THE CONTROLLER AND OF THE PAPER CONTROL TRIBUNAL CONFIRMED AND EXTENDED.
speechtext:
I am quite well aware that only a part of the revenue of the Laurentide Company comes from the sale of newsprint. But I see no reason for the most unwarranted and unjust attack which was made upon the Government by the managing director of the Laurentide Company when he had, as a matter of fact, a statement the best by far that he had ever been able to show to his shareholders -I think a million dollars more profit than he had before. Who was hurt in this matter? In war time does any body suppose that an appeal to this House and to the country is likely to have weight and validity if the parties making it say: It is true we made a million dollars more than we did the year before, but we might have made a great deal more but for the action of the Government? The Government in this matter had to see that something like justice was done-and we did. There is no political gain from that. You never gain anything from what you have done; it is only to-morrow that counts in politics. There is no gratitude for what a Government has done; there is only expectation of what it may do. Speaking for myself, from the political standpoint, I would rather never have had anything to do with She thing. We did it. We appointed Mr. . Pringle, and Mr. Pringle, as a judicial officer, fixed the price, which price is now before an appeal court of three judges of undoubted standing. As far as I can see, the action of the Government has been one of scrupulous justice between the two interests. Nothing else could be done if the press of this country was not to be put out of existence. Apart from war jurisdiction, it would not be a good thing for this country that there should be only a few wealthy newspapers. One of the safeguards of political freedom is the fact that we have Hundreds of small newspapers throughout this country which can take any editorial course of action they desire. That is a good thing. The ordinary newspaper man is not a business man at all. He usually is busy carrying on his paper, and When he looks at his balance sheet at the end of the year he finds very little profit indeed. A

few newspapers could have stood the high price of newsprint. But what would have been the effect nationally as the result of the situation that would have developed from our non-interference? You would have only a few newspapers that were rich enough to stand during the period of the war, notwithstanding the price of newsprints, and the others would be put out of business. That would not be good for the public life of this country.
My hon. friend has spoken about the press in the United States and Mr. Imrie in going down to Washington. I have no control over Mr. Imrie. This is a free country, and it was open to him or to any other member of the Canadian Press Association to go down there and take part in the proceedings. * My hon. friend himself could have gone down if he so desired. But I want to point out that the publishers of this country have an immediate interest in the price paid for newsprint in the United States, because in ordinary times the price paid here is determined by the price paid . there. Obviously, if you have a price, say, of $70 a ton in the United States, the manufacturers here are going to sell all their product there if the price here is not equal to the United States price. In other words, the price in the United States has a re-active effect upon the price in Canada; and therefore the newspaper publishers of this country have an interest in the price which is paid in the United States. Let us assume a case, I do not say it exists at all-I have been very fair in my statement with respect to combines. I never make a statement that there is a combine unless I have incontrovertible proof, and I do not think any one should, and I have not proof that there is a combine-but supposing there was a combine between the newsprint manufacturers of Canada and of the United States, and let us say they fixed the price in the United States at $80 a ton, where it should be $60 a ton. Does my hon. friend mean to say that the publishers of this country would not be interested in the fact that there was a combine, and that they would have to pay $80 a ton instead of $60? That is the position.
I want to say to my hon. friend that the Government has acted throughout this matter as guardians of the public interest, and not as a Government under intimidation by newspapers. It was a most monstrous statement to make that this Government acted under any such intimidation, and I resent it very strongly. There is not any one living who can intimidate me

or this Government. There is not enough in public life for any man of spirit to allow himself to be intimidated. We have carried this out because we considered it our duty to carry it out. If the same situation arose to-morrow I would do the same thing.

The fact that such concerns as the Laurentide made money is that they derive a large part of their revenue from the Shawindgan water-power, and in addition to that they make .a hundred tons of sulphite pulp per day that this Government did not fix the price on. The company I have the honour to be president of does not make any sulphite pulp; it has to buy it. And, Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of this House, would you be surprised to hear that the sulphite pulp we bought to put into the manufacture of our paper that we had to sell at $50 a ton. cost us $70 a ton? Fortunately only twenty-five per cent of news paper is sulphite, the remaining seventy-five per cent is ground wood. Nevertheless, if the Government was going to fix the price of paper, why did they not fix the price on the whole line of paper? But that is not all. Here is the seiious part
of this business. The fact of the Canadian manufacturers having to supply paper at $7.50 a ton less than actual cost is not so serious a matter as the fact that eighty-nine per cent is sold elsewhere, principally in the United States. The publishers of the United States are practically the same class of people as we have here-they are clamouring for cheaper material, and when this Government fixed the price of paper to be supplied to the press of Canada at $2.50 .per hundred pounds, the publishers of the United States went to their Government and they said: Here, why do you allow the Canadian manufacturers to come into the United States and sell us paper at three and a half and four cents a pound when the Government of their own country says that two and a half cents a pound is a fair price? The outcome of that has been that the manufacturers of Canada have had to fight for their existence. We have had to spend over $500,000 in defending our. selves. I want to tell the minister, I do not know whether he will like it or not, that the press of Canada convinced the .Government that- the Government were going out of existence instead of the press if they did not concede its wishes and demands. speechtext: Well, this Government is a political institution. There was the greatest exhibition of politics in this House last night that I ever saw in my life. speechtext:

Would it not be well to have these experts appointed by the Governor in Council when the necessity for their appointment is shown by a report of the board to the Governor in Council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The board, of course, could not report to the Governor in Council. Only the minister can do that, but the proof of the occasion requiring it would come from the board, and the minister would base his report to council upon the report from the board.

Well, then, upon a report to the Prime Minister. The clause says:
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, or as the occasion requires, appoint one or more experts or persons having technical or special knowledge of the matters in question, to assist in an advisory capacity in respect of any matter before the board.
'Would it not be well to have the appointments subject to a demand from the board?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hopp the hon. member will realize that no Prime Minister would appoint experts unless he had some report from the board indicating that they were necessary.

We are always acting on assumptions. Why not have it put in the Act? It may be all very well for the Prime Minister to say he would make no appointment unless he had received a report from the board, but this board is appointed for a special purpose and the minister, in this case the Prime Minister, is to be a kind of supervisor of the board. I do not think it would hurt to have that stated in the Bill.
Mr. iMoMASTER:	Would the minister
explain why such experts would, not be appointed by the Civil Service Commission?
I noticed the Civil Service Commission advertising the other day even for a man as expert as one learned in law. When the minister wanted a solicitor for his department he had to go to the Civil Service Commission -to get one, and by a strange coincidence the Civil Service -Commission furnished him with the very man he wanted.
. I-f the 'Civil Service Commission undertakes to select men who have such special qualifications as lawyers -must have, why is the choice of experts required by this board- not left to the Civil -Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The experts as contemplated here will be appointed merely for a temporary period-a cost accountant, or a man of that kind. No appointments under
this A-ct would come under the Civil Service Commission, not even the staff.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If they are permanent, the Civil Service Act would apply.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: 'The bid Act applies in any event. I am quite prepared to have the Civil Service Adt apply in the case of these appointments as in the case of any others.

speechtext:
I think the board
themselves should call in the experts they

require. If this board is to be of the importance of the Railway Commission and we are to have the confidence in it that we have in the Railway Commission, I think we should trust them with the appointment of such experts as they may require in their investigations all over the country. The Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior know very well that whenever a judge sitting in admiralty wants an assessor to sit with him on the bench he has power under the law to call him in, and the assessor sits' with him and advises him on [DOT]expert questions. If this hoard is going to travel all over the country it would be very awkward when they wanted an expert to have to communicate with Ottawa. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman's
reasoning is wrong for the reason that his premise is wrong. In the event of the Railway Commission requiring an expert they go to the 'Governor in Council; in fact, this clause down to the word " board " is precisely the same as clause 21 of the Railway Act, which is the corresponding clause as regards the Railway Commission.
The principle is that the Governor in Council must exercise a supervision over expenditure. They cannot be allowed do write cheques against the Treasury at will. The latter part is as to the establishment-*of an advisory council to the board. It is unpaid.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand this section to mean that experts would te called in to deal with special cases. Perhaps the minister will explain.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I said before that they were temporary ^ and I still think it is better for the Governor in Council to exercise supervision, otherwise you would be enabling the body itself to write cheques against the treasury without any oversight from responsible administration. It is the very same with the Railway Commission, and I do not think that this body should

be put on a higher status than the Railway Commission.
I do not know that the minister has explained why persons "skilled and experienced in matters affecting industry" who may be named by the advisory council to assist them, should be unpaid.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As to the advisory council, the precedent for that is in connection with the Food Board. They had an advisory council unpaid. They were not put to any expense, and much was not asked of them. It did good work. In dealings affecting a certain trade there might be a man especially acquainted with that trade whose advice would be of very great use. Such men were used to advantage in connection with the Food Board, and the idea of the draftsman was that the same course might be followed here. There is no need for pay.

speechtext: It would not do any harm. I thought it was rather remarkable to allow the commissioners to reside within five miles.
