On section 19-Salary of commissioners:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I had the Bill printed without salaries being inserted. I beg to move-and I do so for the purpose of discussion in Committee; I think it is a subject for discussion, and I am not wedded to any particular figures1-that the salary of the chief commissioner be fixed at $7,000, and the salary of the other two commissioners at $6,000 each. The Prime Minister reminds me that it will require a resolution to make provision for the payment of these salaries. However, I suggest these salaries for discussion and I beg to move as follows:	,
That sub-clause (3) be repealed and the following substituted therefor:
Such salaries shall ibe paid monthly out of such moneys as Parliament may appropriate for the purpose.	\
Then I propose to move that the words "seven thousand" be inserted in line 34, and the words "six thousand" in line 35.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That would not be in order at the present stage unless the hon. gentleman first proceeds by way of resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is in order, I understand, providing sulb-clause 3 is changed, because the salaries must be appropriated by Parliament before they can be paid.
For the purpose of comparison I would like to know what the salary of the Chief Railway Commissioner is:

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The salary of the Chief Railway Commissioner was originally fixed,
I think, at $10,000. Some years ago it was raised to $12,000 which is the amount he draws now. The other commissioners draw $8,000 each, except the assistant chief commissioner, who is paid $9,000.

If you fix the salary of your chief commissioner at $7,000, will you not run a risk of creating a feeling of soreness in the minds and hearts of all your deputy ministers? There is, for example, the Deputy Minister of Public Works who is entrusted with responsibility for millions and millions of dollars, and there is the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries. It does seem to me that the salary of a man who is the head of a purchasing commission should not be bigger than that of a deputy minister. When it is remembered that the stipend of Solicitor General, a position which has been occupied by men of great eminence and learning in this country, is only $5,000 a year it does seem to me that the salary proposed in this case is a large one.

It is a Board of Commerce which is to be appointed under the Bill, and not a purchasing commission. This board demands men of as great capacity as we have in this country -
Mr. JACOBS': Hear, hear.

-or else we are going to have trouble. I do not think the salaries mentioned by the minister are sufficient to secure the services of the type of men that we require for this board. I think the salaries paid to its members should be equal to those which the judges in the higher courts enjoy. My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) suggests the salaries paid to the judges of the Court of Appeal

or the Supreme Court, for purposes of comparison. That may be, personally I do not know how to designate the courts because I do not appear in them any oftener than I can help.
You will have to go there oftener.

I would suggest that the initial salary for the chief should be at least $8,000 and $7,000 for each assistant.
Mr. JAC0RS: I would go even further than the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nesbitt). I have always gone on the principle that it is necessary in making appointments of this kind to secure the very best men that can possibly be got. You cannot induce any person of eminence to leave his profession, or his business, and enter the Government's service for such a sum as $8,000 a year. I have in mind, of course, the fact that many of our judges are glad to ascend the Bench for a salary of seven or eight thousand dollars a year; but here we are appointing an entirely new board and it seems to me that if the Chief Railway Commissioner receives $12,000 a year salary, the president of this board should commence with a stipend of $10,000 a least. Otherwise, we will have applicants for the position who would be nothing more nor less than failures in their own business, and we certainly ought not to inaugurate the creation of this board by appointing men of that kind. Of course, the Government may have in mind the appointment of ministers who are about to retire from the Cabinet, or other people for whom it is seeking to obtain positions.

I think the minister is on pretty safe ground in adhering to the salaries he proposes, rather than to adopt the suggestions of hon. gentlemen who have spoken on this subject, and who have advocated that higher stipends shall be paid. There is one thing we may rest assured of: If the salaries are found to be inadequate, it will be a very easy matter, judging from past experience, to augment them-
Mr. JACOB'S: Not too easy.

-but a very difficult matter to lower them if they are once placed too high. I think it is a very serious reflection on the judiciary of this country in my opinion, entertaining as I do a very high regard for that judiciary-
Oh, oh.

-to say that a salary of $7,000 will only attract to the Bench men

of mediocre ability. We have many judges in Canada who are not drawing salaries any higher than that, and who, I believe, would fill these positions with eminent satisfaction. In rriy opinion there are lots of men. in the Dominion who would be glad to accept the position of chief commissioner, proposed under this Bill, at the salary suggested. If you make the salary any higher there will be a terrible scramble, and the-worries of the Government, which are already great enough, will be greatly magnified. It is a funny thing, but it seems to be the fact, that the higher you fix the salaries attached to these positions the larger the number of men that apparently are qualified to fill them, judging from the rush that takes place when vacancies have to be filled or appointments have to be made. I think. there has been too much of a general tendency to add to the salaries of men who are already being paid far more than they are worth, if we consider, the duties they discharge as compared with what other men are doing.
Hear, hear.
There "has been too much of a disposition to augment the salaries of men who are getting five times the amount: paid to others who are doing just as good and efficient work.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) will admit there is some distinction between a judge on the Bench and the President of this Board. A judge has a certain position of dignity in the community which is given to him merely by the fact that he occupies a seat on the Bench. I have in mind the case of Mr. James B. Dill, who was at one time chief counsel for the United States Steel Company, and who organized that gigantic trust. Mr. Dill was appointed Chief Justice of New Jersey, where he receives the munificent salary of, I believe, $3,000, whereas formerly he must have earned $500,000 as a practising lawyer. But he was willing to accept the office simply because of the fact that it was a position of great prominence and he wished to be Chief Justice to round off his career.
I wish to resent the statement made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Edwards) that there is any reflection upon the judiciary in my remarks, when I said you cannot get the best men for a paltry salary. I have always taken the ground in this House that the judges of the high courts should receive a larger salary than they are now getting, which is entirely inadequate. When we are creating these new positions of such importance.

we ought to see that we make the salaries attractive. Although there may be a scramble for the chief commissionership, we must have the very best man possible for such a position, if the duties of the office are to be carried out properly.
Personally, I may say that I am entirely against the organization of this board at the present juncture, and that is not only my own view but the view of very many people inside the House and out of it, and if I may be permitted, I would like to read a letter which has been addressed to me on the subject by the Montreal Board of Trade.
I would have read it yesterday but I was called away from Ottawa, and this is the first opportunity I have since had of doing so. The letter in question reads as fqllows:
The Montreal Board of Trade,
Montreal, July 2, 1919.
Dear Sir,
I am directed to ask for your support of this hoard's protest against the- enactment of legislation creating a Board of Commerce during the last few days of the present session of Parliament, and without the public, who are so vitally interested, being afforded an opportunity to consider the provisions of the Government's proposal.
The following telegram was to-day addressed to the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, Premier-
"Montreal Board of Trade protests most -strongly against passage of. legislation creating Board of Commerce in closing days of session and without affording the public opportunity of studying provisions of a measure of such importance. Board urges that Bill be printed and circulated as widely as possible and that consideration thereof by Parliament be deferred till next session."
I am, dear Sir,
Yours truly,
J. Stanley Cook, Assistant Secretary.
S. L. Jacobs, M.P.
That expresses the opinions of people whose views, I think, ought to be considered valuable, not only here but throughout the country. I am pretty sure it is also the view of many other large bodies and corporations in the country.

I do not want to take up the time of the Committee but I think you really will not get the type of men you require for this board unless the salaries are made sufficiently large. So far as our judges are concerned the remuneration they *enjoy is little enough for the high type of men necessary for such positions and very frequently we do not get the right kind of man that is needed. I am not saying anything against the judiciary, but very frequently the higher class of men are not willing to leave their professions in order to ascend the Bench.
This is a very, very important thing that we are doing here to-day. It is all very well to say there will be a scramble for the positions. There may be a scramble for a certain type of >
men, but they .are not the type of men, as I understand, that the Government want to appoint. Therefore, I think the very lowest figure at which the Government should fix these salaries is what I have suggested, $8,000 and $7,000.
I would be in .accord with my hon. friend who has just sat down (Mr. Jacobs) that we put the chief commissioner at $10,000, if it is satisfactory to the House, because of the fact that I want the best man we can get to preside over this board; otherwise we are going to have tremendous trouble For these positions we want broad, liberal-minded men, men. of knowledge, men who have had business experience, and therefore I do not believe that we will want to appoint men who will scramble for the positions-the position ought to seek the man in this case.
Mr. LALOB; I quite agree with the remarks of the member for Oxford North (Mr. Nesbitt). This is a very important commission and I think you want the best men that can be got for the positions, .and therefore the salaries should be sufficient to induce men. of the proper standing to accept these responsibilities. I think the man at the head of this commission, should be paid $10,000v I do not think that $6,000 or $7,000 is sufficient to attract the right class of men. There will be a great scramble for this position among men who are probably worth $7,000, but the man we want to apply for it is the $10,000 man.
We do not want him to seek the position; we want the position to seek him.

It is the same as in one's own business, the best man you can get is the cheapest man, and for a position of this kind I think $10,000 'is not too much.
Mr. JACOBS; Possibly the Government expects that this board will be able to so reduce the cost of living that $7,000 and $6,000 will be attractive.

When I spoke last, Mr. Chairman, I did not appreciate that this is to be a court. Being a court, I cannot very well see how the minister can be prepared to pay the professional members of that court a higher salary than is paid to the judges of other courts. I am afraid he would find himself in hot water with all the judges if he started at the inception of

this court to put its professional members on a higher plane as regards salary than other judges.

What about the Chief Commissioner of the Railway Commission?
Mr. McMA^TER: True; but the value_of that commission to the country has probably justified the high salary paid. But as the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has very well said, it is easier to put salaries up than to bring them down, and I am inclined to think that the suggestion of the minister is a proper one and that it should be accepted (by the House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: After hearing the views of the Committee my intention was to have this clause stand. I may say to the hon. member for Brome that consideration for the feelings of the judges towards myself and the fear of bringing down their ire will not have very great effect, because I am in that position now.
So am I.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is another thing to be considered in connection with judges' salaries,-a judge goes to the bench usually after a good many years' active practice, he accepts the high office as a life work, and at the end of his judicial career, if it is terminated by physical disability, or if it extends to the period of fifteen years or more, he retires with a pension. But this is a very different position, and I should hope that no judge would feel aggrieved by the fact that a higher salary was given for discharging duties of this character which are essentially different from the work of a judge. I think the Acting Minister of Justice is well advised to let the clause stand so as to consider the suggestions which have been made. I was a good deal impressed by what was said by my hon. friend from George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) and by the hon. member for Oxford North (Mr. Nesbitt), and the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Lalor). It has been repeatedly said in this House and in this Committee that the utility of this legislation will depend very largely indeed on the quality of the men who are selected to give effect to it. It might be difficult for the Government to obtain the service of men of the quality desired without fixing the standard of remuneration somewhat higher than that proposed by the minister.
Section stands.

On section 20-Salaries of staff how fixed:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will the appointments to this board be subject to the decision of the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am advised that the Civil Service Act applies without any special reference to it in this Bill. However, I am quite prepared that a clause be added to the Bill to provide that the Civil Service Act shall apply.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 22-Salaries to be voted by Parliament:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: We passed- the question of salaries, but I wish to ask the minister what advantage does he think he is going to get by having three commissioners instead of one. I am sure that if a man is going to sit as a court investigating cases coming before him on evidence, he is a much more effective court than a court composed of three men. A personnel of three or four is all right for a Court of Appeal, .but in the case of a trial court it is infinitely better to have one man than three.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That point has, I think, given me more concern than any other phase of this Act. Indeed, I did have clauses drafted at one time providing for a court of one alone. But after consultation with' other members of the Government and with hon. members of the House I came to the conclusion that it was better to recommend to Parliament a court of three. The reasons are these: First, it is very probable that members of the court will require to be in different parts of the country at the same time, for the same reason that different members of the Railway Commission are required to be in different parts of the country at the same time. Secondly, if there is but one commissioner and he is a judge, then the other elements of the population are not represented. It is more appropriate that in a court of this kind there should be an infusion of the business element, because it is a business court; and, if possible, of the labour element, as peculiarly representing that portion of the consumers mostly affected. It will be very difficult, I know, to include in a court of three such men as can be said to represent wholly and adequately all portions of the population first affected, but the best will be done that can be done. Any way, you can do it better with a court of three than with a court of one. Lastly, it is felt that the attitude of the public

toward the court will be better, the degree of confidence reposed in it by the people will be higher, if the court is composed of three than if it is composed of one.

Has the Government in
view the appointment of at least one member of the board who can speak the two official languages?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That point came up
yesterday, and I realize the importance of the suggestion. But if you must have a man who can speak both French and English, a ipan who will represent labour, a man who will represent business, a man who will represent, perhaps, the returned soldiers, it will be difficult to get a man who will fulfil all these requirements. But the best will be done that can be done.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 25-jurisdiction:

Is it proposed to have a
special prosecutor or investigator attached to this board?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not at its inception at any rate. In my own judgment-and for the information of my hon. friend (Mr. Vien), I may say, in the judgment of the draftsman'-there is no prospective need now for such an official, though one may ultimately become necessary. But we are very anxious to avoid being legitimately charged with seeking to create an office for a friend.
That is the charge, anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know that we shall be charged with it, anyway, but people will put no stock in that charge. It is believed that there is no need of relieving the provincial authorities of the responsibility of prosecuting, particularly when the Dominion goes to the extent of picking out the offender, securing the evidence, and handing it on to the Attorney General of the province.
How do they propose to pick out the offenders under this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is the province of this board. Having found that a man or a company is violating its rules as to fair prices and good business practice, the board secures the evidence and hands it over, with the name of the man or the company and all other necessary information, to the Attorney General. All the Attorney General has to do is to present these facts to a court, and if he can show that the offender violated
an order of this board, the offender must be found guilty. *
Would not an amendment to the Criminal Code effect all that, without the necessity of a board ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no. This has to do with some remarks made by the member for Kent (Mr. McCoig), who seemed to think that if you simply appointed a Crown prosecutor and told him to go after people, everything would be all right. But you must have legislation which defines what the offences are; otherwise, what is the Crown prosecutor or anybody else going to do? The legislation which is to be introduced following this Bill will define what constitute offences, based on the principle that the board, after investigating a given case, can fix the line of conduct that individuals, companies or sets of people must pursue, and if they do not pursue that line of conduct they are offenders.
The Act passed a few years ago in connection with combines and restraints of trade is . operated now under the sections of the Criminal Code, and the local courts have jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but that Act is inoperative because there is no continuing body, no watch-dog at the gate, to see that if one order is evaded another is passed to deal with the situation, and that if orders are persistently evaded, the matter may be referred to the Attorney General for action. This board is empowered by the State to perform just that task. If one order is evaded, another is passed which the offender cannot evade; or, if he succeeds in evading it, another is passed, and all the time publicity gathers round him and he cannot very well escape from it. It is partly in that way that the correction which we seek will be gained.
If a firm charged with profiteering is brought before this commission, I assume that that person or firm may employ counsel to present their side of the case?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

And the case is then to be tried by this board only to the extent of determining whether or not a true bill can be found against the person or firm concerned. If they find sufficient evidence to convince them that the person or firm has been guilty, they hand the matter over to the Attorney General who hands it over to

some judge, and then I presume they would have the right to bring their proof up again before the court, and the final adjudicature would take place before the court and not before the commission. In other words, the commissioners could not carry the matter to a finality.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In most respects the
hon. member is right, but there is one fundamental fact that he o'mits. If a charge of unfair prices is made against a firm, and a commissioner is convinced that there is sufficient evidence to warrant an investigation, he issues an order .upon that firm to appear and defend itself, and the investigation takes place. The chief commissioner has to raitfy the order. After investigation, if the evidence is sufficient to warrant it in the opinion of the commissioners, they issue an order restraining the man from following that practice; they define the limits within which he may gp. If he disobeys that order, he is guilty of an offence and liable to the penalty herein imposed. The facts are then submitted to the Attorney General with the names of the witnesses and of the man who is accused, and all that the Attorney General has to do is to present those facts to the court and show by those facts that that man has disobeyed an order issued against him by this board. The court does not try the matter all over again; the court has nothing whatever to say as to whether the order is right or not; all that the court inquires into is whether the man obeyed the order of the board or nbt. If he disobeyed it, the man is guilty of an offence.

The jurisdiction
seems 'to be limited according to the Bill as I understand it. Clause 27 says:
The board may, of its own motion, or shall upon the request of the minister inquire into, hear and determine any matters or things which under this Act, or under the special Act, it may inquire into.
That means that the board has the right, if it knows of a violation of the law, to commence proceedings of its own motion. It also has the right, when the minister makes a reference to the board, but it does not give the ordinary citizen, who has a complaint against any particular branch of trade, the right to write a letter or to make a complaint direct to the board. He has got to go to the minister, and the-minister might or might not give permission to the ordinary man who wants to have a complaint investigated. I can imagine such circumstances in which the minister might not grant permission. Any

citizen of Canada who has a complaint -against railway freight rates or any other question coming within the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission, can write a letter to that pommission and have the matter investigated and adjusted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. member is. referring to. Certainly the ordinary citizen can come to this board and ask for an investigation; the Government does not control the board nor the citizen. 1

What is the
section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the specific
section in that regard is in -the Combines and Fair Prices Act, but there is nothing here to restrain .a citizen. Is the hon. member referring to section 25?
Section 27.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are only at section 25 yet. I will speak to section 27 when we reach it.

Supposing the Railway Commission issue an order and that order is disobeyed. Would they deal with the offender regarding that, and if they do, why should not this board be constituted with the same powers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They do not. If the
Railway Commission did that, they would have to have a set of sheriffs, bailiffs and constables. As regards a man who violates an order of the Railway Commission, there is provision made for his prosecution, for correction, for following him up, but the Railway Commission have not an organization to do that. That is done through the ordinary process just the same as this.

Am I right in
supposing that this board has no power to enforce its own orders, and that they must be enforced by the courts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

As regards what the hon. member (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) said, clause 6 of Bill No. 167, states:
Any British subject, resident in Canada and of full age, who is of opinion that a combine exists or is being formed may apply in writing to any member of the board	
' The application, as I understand it, is made direct to the commissioner, although it may be made to the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. In further reply to the hon. member for Frontenae (Mr. Edwards) an order of this board may be made

a rule of the Exchequer 'Court, or of any court. The procedure is defined in the Act as simply taking the order before the court and making it a rule of the court. Then immediately the machinery of that court, criminal and civil, is at the disposal of the board for the enforcement of its authority, instead of duplicate machinery being established.

Section 25 seems to be merely administrative; it is not compulsory for the board to do certain things. I had the impression that the object of this Bill was to form a commission, the members of which would have to investigate certain
4 p.m. conditions in business houses.
Under this Bill they are simply given the power to do certain things; I think it ought to be stated that the jurisdiction should be a duty imposed upon them to investigate business dealings of commercial houses. Is not that the purpose of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the Bill, too.
That is not what it says.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The word " may " must be used because you cannot put it into the power of any crank to come to the board and compel an investigation where there is no cause for it. You must place it within the discretion of the board to say whether that investigation takes place or not. 'Consequently, the word " may " is used, but they are charged with that duty.

My objection is that they are not charged with the duty. This simply means that the board is constituted and may or may not, as it sees fit, investigate any particular business. That is not the purpose of this Bill; its purpose is that the board shall investigate so many times during the year every concern carrying on business in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Yes. The duty of this board is surely, if it has any duty at all, to find out whether any profiteering is going on, if any excess profits are being made. If the board is going to do any effective work it should have a board of examiners on its staff to go into any person's office and say: We want to examine your books in order to see what profits you are going to make out of your business. If this board is to be constituted and is merely to sit down and wait until somebody comes in and makes a complaint, that is, so to speak, passing the buck. It ought to be the primary duty of
this board to investigate once or twice each year every mercantile institution in this country, to send its examiners in and say: We want to see your books in order to find out what profits you are making. Otherwise you will simply have a commission that will never do anything unless a complaint is made. People object to making complaints because they have to assume a certain responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know what appropriation the hon. member would be ready to make to this board, but they would need something like the demobilization vote to do the work he seems to think they should perform. Why, the courts of the provinces are commissioned to try offenders, but they are not instructed to go around to the home of every citizen and inquire what each did all the year round to find out whether he committed an offence or not. This board is charged and directly charged with the enforcement of the 'Combines and Fair Prices Act. It can act upon information given to it, or of its own motion. How can you go any further than that?

What was our experience under the old Combines Act? It has been in force for the last fifteen years but there have been only two prosecutions under it, one the prosecution of a grocer in Ontario. The same thing will happen in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That old Act was a failure.	,
Mr, FRIPP: Yes, for the reason I mentioned. No one would take the responsibility of laying information. I say it should be the duty of the board of its own motion to start these investigations.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So it will, if it has any reason to believe that offences have been committed.
Who is going to give them reason to believe offences have been committed?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I must assume the hon. member's well known powers of reasoning have not deserted him. Surely he does not suggest that this board .must investigate every institution in Canada, big or small, whether they have any reason to suspect that an offence has been committed or not. Surely he does not suggest that this should be continually digging at the roots of our industrial life. I could not describe such a suggestion as that. It is true that the old Combines Act was not a success partly for the reason the hon. member



gives, but mainly for t/h'e reason that when it was in vogue adequate remedies could not be reached. I have given twice to the committee what in my judgment was the secret of the difficulty, namely, the absence of a sort of judicial police, a continuing body in pursuit, to watch for evasions and stop escapes. In this Bill we-provide that, and we provide full power for the board to act of its own motion. There is no possibility of going further.

It seems to me there is some difference between the powers given to this board and the powers given to the Railway Commission. The Railway Commission, as I understand it, when it finds certain conditions, orders certain things to be done, and has power to enforce its orders. For instance, a short time ago in the West we had trouble over cattle getting on the railway tracks through their not being fenced, and a great many cattle were killed. Complaints were laid, and the Railway Commission ordered the railways f to fence their tracks. I remember very well that in one case the chairman of the commission stated to the railway company: "I order you to build that fence by such a time." Has this -board similar powers to make orders, and to see they are enforced?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. The way the Railway Commission enforces its orders, in general-I will not go into any particular case -is by making its orders a rule of the court, and then the machinery of the courts of the country are at its disposal to enforce that order. That is exactly the case here. An order of this board can be made a rule of the court, and thereupon it is a mandatory order of the -court enforceable through the machinery of the court.
Who will pay the expenses of the execution of that order?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The court.

I am in agreement with my hon. friend (Mr. Fripp) that if this board is going to do any good it will have to be aggressive; it will have to look for violations of the laiw. If it waits until complaints are made, it will do very little good because complaints may not come to the board. The board should go in search of violations of the law. My hon. friend knows what is taking place in connection with prosecutions under the Inland Revenue Department. To-day special detectives are going around the whole of Nova Scotia calling on the small dealers and buy-
IMr. Meiglien.]
ing a tin of talcum powder or something of that kind to see if the stamp is put on, and there are frequent prosecutions under the law. This board should search out violations of the law in just the same way.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member's idea is perfectly right. The, only statement he made that was wrong was when he said he was in agreement with my hon. friend (Mr. Fripp). He is not at all. It is certainly the duty of this board to go into the highways and byways to find offences; it is empowered and directed to see that there shall be no violations of the -Combines and Fair Prices Act. But we are not embodying in the Act a mandatory order that the board must investigate the business of every person in Canada.
I do not think my hon. friend need worry about complaints. There will be plenty of complaints laid; the only question will be whether there is any basis for them.

I think my hon. friend from Guysborough is mixing two things that are not alike. The cases he mentioned were charges of defrauding the revenue by not putting on the necessary stamps. The public is not very much interested in that. A nearer parallel would have been the enforcement of the Criminal Code. How are prosecutions started under the Criminal -Code? Almost always by information laid by a private citizen, and any of u-s who have had to- do with the enforcement of the code know that we have not so much trouble in getting complaints, as in checking them up. There are a good many busy-bodies going around making complaints which never should be made. There is very little neglect on the part of the public in the matter of laying the necessary information to start proceedings under the Criminal Code, and it strikes me that we shall' have plenty of complaints made under this-Act. Those who -are injured by the actions, of certain firms- will be only too ready to-make complaints. The trouble will be there-will be so many complaints that the board will have to work overtime to investigate-them all.

I think it would improve-the clause if the minister would change the-word "may" in line 27 to "shall." It would then read "the board shall of its own motion or shall upon the request of the minister." I think that would fulfil the desire of several hon. members who have spoken, who

think the board should act upon the complaint of any citizen. '
If a citizen complained to the Prime Minister it is highly probable that, should he come to the conclusion that there was something in the complaint, he would make a request to the board, as contained in the second line of the clause. I think that the Act could be improved and the minister would attain the result he manifestly desires, if we made it compulsory for the board to act, rather than to leave it optional by the use of the permissive " may." There is no doubt that some of these boards that are created do get somnolent at times and do not act unless there is some definite complaint. If we use the word " shall," then after the discussion we have had here, it will be clear to the board that their duty is to investigate without waiting.

speakerposition: Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The wording of this Bill seems to be taken very largely from the Railway Act. The Railway Act provides that the board " shall have full jurisdiction to inquire into, hear, and determine any application by or on behalf of any party interested " who complains that any company or person has failed to observe certain regulations. This says that the board shall have jurisdiction to investigate, inquire, etc., under the Combines Act, so that it is practically identical with the Railway Act. I do not think that any one will charge the Railway Commission with having failed to fulfil all the obligations that were expected of them. That Act is one that redounds to the credit of the late Administration, and there has never been a body that has given more satisfaction than the Railway Commission. Exactly the same procedure is required in this case as in the case of the Railway Commission. If the suggestion of the hon. member for Parkdale were adopted, it would simply mean that on some man in a by-town writing a post card to the commission that John Smith had been guilty of profiteering, the commission would have to investigate, and they might be engaged ih a wild goose chase all the time. If there is a case of profiteering and reasonable evidence is brought before the commission, they will not be doing their duty if they do not investigate it. But I think that a prima facie case should at least be made out.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 27-may inquire into any matter referred to it, etc.:
289J
This clause does not seem to be satisfactorily worded. It says that the board may " of its own motion, or shall upon the request of the minister

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is in regard to inquiries on the part of the Government. There is a clause in the 'Combines Act in regard to inquiries by individuals. If the word " shall " were substituted for " may ", the board would have to inquire into the business of some little comer candy store in Cape Breton, say. With the word " may ", it has power to do so, but if the other word were inserted the board might be compelled to go and examine into trifling ipatters and waste its time all the year round. Its duty is to prevent excess profits, and the only way in which it can perform that duty satisfactorily is to aot when it has good reason to do so.
You could provide that the board " shall when it believes that there is good ground ", and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is exactly what this means. They may do it.
I gather from the minister's remarks that this board will not have any machinery but is going to be entirely dependent on the individual, the consumer for information.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
That is the impression-I have gathered so far.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You should read the Bill.
It leaves it te the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the board " may, of its own motion ", without any one saying anything; and it " shall " upon the request of the minister.
Who is going to bring the information to the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the information
doesn't come to the minister it will go to>
the board, and if it does not it is the duty of the board to find it out. But you cannot compel the board to go into every corner of the country to hold investigations without reason.
I am not going so far. From what source do you expect to derive your information?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The board will be composed of human beings the same as the rest

of us. The hon. member belongs to that class. Has he not within the last six months got information that would induce him, if lie were empowered and if it were his sworn duty to do so, to investigate this, that or *the other thing? The board will get this information in the same way, perhaps not by formal application and perhaps not even by letter. But it will get this information under a constantly operating machinery *and a system of inquiry which the board doubtless will constitute, because the Act makes provision whereby they can obtain from every "person doing business in the country any information they require as to cost, expenses, selling price, goods in store, etc. They will always have before them an array of facts as to individuals that will enable them to decide where special investigation is needed.

Change that word to
" shall," and you will have effective machinery.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If tlie word " shall "
is used instead of " may " the commission will have to ipry into everybody's business even if they see no cause whatever.

Not at all.
, Mr. MEIGHEN:	Certainly. The word
" may " means exactly the same as " shall, if they see cause." We tell them it is their duty to keep down unfair prices and we give them certain powers by the use of the word " may." If we use the word " shall " they will have no discretion and will have to be digging at the roots of the business of every person. In that way 'they will only dissipate their energies without any good cresult.

They must be supposed
to be reasonable men. There is a difference between the two words. If you say that the board " shall," when they have reason "to believe that action is necessary, you do *not make it compulsory for them to investigate without cause. It would be absurd to suppose that the board would investigate without complaint. It seems to me the Bill would better carry out the manifest intention if we used the word " shall." They would act when they saw cause.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is precisely what
is provided. They are directed to act in such a case. They have to do their duty.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 32-stating a case for the Supreme 'Court of Canada:
X Mr. Meighen. ]
What will be the offences under this Act? Will they only have relation to combines? For example, .what does profiteering mean?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is defined by the next Bill, No. 167. The offences are constituted under it and it is that Act which this board is directed to enforce. It is the duty of this board to enforce the Combines and Fair Prices Act.
That is putting the cart before the horse?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, this is the horse that draws the cart.

speechtext: The offences.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 36-interim ex parte orders may be granted:
Mr. ARlCHAMBAULT: Why not provide for a period of delay in connection with this clause? It reads:
but no such interim order shall be made for any longer time than the board may deem necessary to enable the matter to toe heard and determined.
Why not provide for a delay of ten days or two weeks for the interim order.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course, the circumstances would differ in every case. For example, if, on affidavit or otherwise, it were shown that some practice was impending; or some combination was being formed, at Vancouver, it would take a considerable time to bring that to the head of an investigation, but if it were at Toronto it would take much less time. A maximum, I suppose, might be fixed, but the board is here directed to allow no further time for the operation of the interim order than is absolutely necessary to hold the investigation. I do not think there could be a more binding provision than that.
Mr. ARlCHAMBAULT: If there was thirty days' delay, surely in that time the board would be able to give proper notice to the company or to the parties interested.

I would point out to the minister that this is an interim ex parte order.
Mr. iMcMASTER: I would suggest that the period should be thirty days.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have no objection to the maximum of thirty .days, but I would be afraid in case it should transpire that the investigation could not be completed in
(


that time. The order would go out of effect and perhaps harm would be done.

It would be
easy during the thirty days to give official notice according to the ordinary procedure.

It would remain an
interim order but it would be no longer an ex parte order. Thirty days should be long enough in the case of an order that is interim and ex parte.
And the interim order can be removed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Thirty days or even,
thirty-five may not be enough, and it must be the least possible time that would serve.

I think we should amend
this clause so as to provide:
iNo Such interim order shall he for any longer time than thirty days.
We must not forget that on any information which may be brought before the court an interim ex parte order will issue directing any concern in Canada to stop during the thing complained of, and when the hearing takes place it may be discovered that there is nothing in the complaint, that the information was wrong. Then if two or three months elapse before the hearing takes place, these people will have been put out of business for that period on a wrong information. It seems to me that for an interim ex parte order a preliminary hearing should take place inside of at least thirty days following the order.

I have drafted a clause here which I think meets the ministers' objection, and it reads as follows:
But no such interim order shall be made for any longer time than the board may deem necessary to enable the parties to be brought before it, and in no case for longer than thirty days.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The difficulty would
be just this: If that clause were to be accepted as it is worded, that immediately the' parties come together and the investigation opens, the interim injunction falls, and they are back just where they were. The investigation might last for two or three weeks. Hon. gentlemen will see the matter must be heard. Once it is heard, then of course the interim injunction shall be made. If it is only to last until they are brought together, harm will be done.

I will meet the minister's objection by providing that no such interim ex parte order shall be made for any longer time than an interim order can
be made for. After that, if the parties have an opportunity of being brougm before the court, they can always be brought before a court in this country within thirty days.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I really think the clause would be better as it is, but I do not want to be obdurate in the matter. If it is to be' altered, it should be rather along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Chambly and Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) because the matter must be determined before any interim order can issue. I would not object, if it is considered better by hon. gentlemen, to inserting this condition at the end of the clause:
Providing no such interim order shall have; effect for a longer period than forty days.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 38-Decision may be made rule or decree of Exchequer Court.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to subparagraphi (5) of this-cl-ause. He said a minute ago that he intended not to provide any special machinery for the execution of the orders of the court, and yet this paragraph says that not only can a judgment of the board be made a rule of the Exchequer Court, but it shall be optional with the board, either before or after its decision or order is made a rule, order or decree of any court, to enforce such decision or order by its own action. Not only can the board make its decision or order become the decision or order of any court of record, but it can also provide-for the necessary machinery-sheriffs, and so forth-for the enforcement of its orders.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is not the effect of sub-clause 5'.
It shall be optional with the board, either before or after its decision or order is made a rule, order or decree of any court,, to enforce-such decision or order by its own action.
That is to say, the decision of the board may be made a rule of court by the action of the board, or anyone interested in it' can proceed and make it a rule of court-Then after it is made a rule of court, the court by its own action can enforce it, but, if so, it utilizes the executive machinery of the courts, and if anybody else wants to enforce it he uses the same executive machinery, just as in the case of an indictment for disobedience of an order.

Does the hon. minister convey the idea that any interested person may request that a rule or. order of the

Efobard become an order or rule of any *court?
iMr. MEIGHEN:	Yes, any person can
'take an order of the board and make it a rule of court.

But it does not say it may be made at the request of any interested party.
Mr. MEIGiHEN: The next section indicates that. Any one may get from the secretary of the board a copy of the order, then he can get that filed and make it a rule of court.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
'On section 41-Appeals from commissioner :

Mr. Chairman, I request the reading of that section.
'The CHAIRMAN: Does the Committee desire that clause 41, a page and a half in length, be read by the Chairman?
Dispensed with.

Mr. Chairman, I request that the clause be read, or that I be allowed time to consider it carefully. This section is most important, for it undoes everything that the Bill has done up to now it gives the Governor in Council power to nullify all the rulings or orders of the board. I think it is only fair and proper that the Committee should read it carefully to know what the enactment is. If the Chairman is too tired on account of the hot weather and the late sittings during the past week, I shall do his duty and read the section to the House.
41. (1) The Governor in Council may, in His discretion, either upon petition of any person interested, lodged within one month after the making of the order, decision, rule or regulation, or within such further time as the board under special circumstances may allow, or of His own motion, at any time, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope and application ; and any order which the Governor in Council may make with respect thereto shall be binding upon the board and upon all Parties.
We will first examine that subsection, Mr. Chairman. We have said repeatedly since the principle of this legislation was introduced that this was simply to throw -dust in the people's eyes, that the Government did not intend to carry out the purposes of the Bill, that it would continue to have direct control over those who had the duty to put this legislation into effect.
iMr, Vien ^
We have given to the hoard the right to regulate, to issue orders and rulings, and to see that such orders and rulings may be made the orders andrulings of the Exchequer Court of Canada or of any other court of record.
By paragraph 1 of this section we give to the Governor in Council the widest power to rescind, to nullify, to destroy the effect of any regulation or ruling of the board. If the board, after full investigation, decided that a certain firm was engaging in unfair commercial practices and issued an order prohibiting those practices, the Government could nullify the action of the board if such ruling or order was directed against some one who was near to the Government. This paragraph is not necessary; it is inconsistent with the general provisions of the Act-and with the Government policy upon which this legislation is based, and for that reason I contend that paragraph 1 of section 41 should be struck out.

I desire to support the
remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Vien). The public is given certain protection with one hand which is take'n away with the other. Why should the Governor in Council interfere with the judgments of this board? Now I can understand why it was first suggested that the members composing this board should receive such modest salaries; the reason is because their judgments are not to be worth the paper they are written on; the Governor in Council can treat any ruling of the board as a mere " scrap of paper." If this provision is adopted, the whole purpose of the Bill is nullified and the enactment is rendered worthless.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This clause received
rather violent criticism yesterday, to which I did not refer in the very few remarks which I made. It was described as " camouflage;" as evidencing clearly that the whole thing was dust in the eyes of the public, even by those who afterwards joined in voting for the Bill.
' I was not here yesterday, so that I cannot be placed in that category.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member would have been a wandering sheep, even if he had been here when we were all unanimous in approval of the Bill.
I might have been a wandering Jew.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A clause similar to
this one was. put in the Act constituting the Railway Commission, and is in it to-

day. The board that we constitute here is not going to have any higher status or any .wider powers than the Railway Commission. It was thought fit when the Act constituting the ^Railway Commission was passed-not for purposes of camouflage or deceit;
I hope hon. members would not suggest that against the immaculate Administration of that day-that this control should be exercised. The reason, in this case as in that, is that the functions of the board, while mainly judicial, are at the same time in a great degree legislative as well; that is to say, a portion of what is ordinary legislative jurisdiction is taken from the Parliament of Canada and placed here. It was thought fit, therefore, when the Railway Board was created seventeen or eighteen years agq, to place a residuary or appellant power in the Governor in Council, exercisable according to such rules as might be thought best and as were proved to be based upon experience. In connection with the administration of the work of the Railway Commission the Governor in Council has followed about this rule, if I am able to define it correctly, they would not interfere with a judgment of the Railway Commission unless it appeared that certain elemental and relevi facts had not been taken into consideration; in which case- -so far as I am aware, always, but I know, very generally-they referred the case back for the renewed consideration of the Railway Commission. Whatever reasons existed for the retention of that appellant or supervisory power over the Railway Commission exists in this case, particularly in the earlier stages of the operation of the Act; it is a sort of balance wheel that may be' called into play where that appears to be absolutely essential in the public, interest. Every year since I have been a membeT of the Government cases have come before it arising out of this provision in the Act creating the Railway Commission. Very rarely is any action taken at all; always, to the best of my recollection, the action taken is a reference back, although there might be cases where there should not be a reference back. I repeat that the principle followed is to interfere only where it appears that important, essential factors in the determination of the matters that were brought before the commission were in some way overlooked or ignored.	[DOT]
There is a court of appeal; why not take cases of that kind to the Supreme Court of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Supreme Court of Canada has jurisdiction only in questions .
of law, in this case as in the case of the Railway Commission. The Governor in Council's jurisdiction is exercised only in questions of fact.
Without having heard the evidence?	(

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have the evidence before us. We do not undertake to determine the credibility of witnesses; that is for the board. The Governor in Council merely says: These men have brought before us relevant facts that did not appear in the record. Or it may be that after the decision of the board is made something happens that causes the carrying out of the order to be against general public policy, in which event it would be wisdom on the part of the Governor in Council to interfere. But the range of cases of interference is very narrow indeed, necessarily so in connection with this board. No Government is going to usurp the functions of the board; such a course would be fatal both to the Government and to the board.
It leaves the door open to criticism.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Every action the Government takes leaves the door open to criticism and to abuse. But for the purposes of correction in special cases such as has been exercised in connection with the operations of the Railway Commission it was deemed wise that this clause, which was embodied there, should be embodied here.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does this provision follow the language of the Act creating the Railway Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

The minister surely does not ignore the difference between the administration of the matters coming under jurisdiction of the Board of Railway 'Commissioners and the administration of the various matters which are to be dealt with by this board. In the operation of the railways of Canada the general policies of the country are involved.
But some private concern may commit offences against Bill No. 167, the Combines and Fair Prices Act, and if they are friends of the Government, they may induce the Government to interfere with the orders of the board, and to rescind or to nullify them, by an Order in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not yet see the reason for the distinction made by the hon. member- I suppose railway men might be friends of the Government, too. In fact, if

my memory serves me aright, I believe I heard hon. gentlemen broadly hinting some time ago that certain railway men were friends of the Government, so that those reasons might possibly exist in the case of the Railway Act just as in this case. Indeed,. railway men might become such friends of the Government that they would be knighted by the Government, and in that case there would be great disposition to interfere. In a word, to repeat, the cases are precisely parallel; whatever reason subsists in the one case subsists in the other.
But two wrongs do not make a right.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is strange that the hon. member will now contend that the evil existed in the other Act.

If the board were to find that certain parties charged had committed a crime by violating the provisions of this Bill, does the minister contend that the Governor in Council would have power to rescind that judgment of the new board ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The board, of course, does not decide that anybody commits a crime; the board decides what is an offence and what is not. It makes the rule, and then the court decides whether or not the rule is violated. If it is, that is an offence against the Act, and once the court decides, the Government, of course, could not interfere.
Between the time the board decided that an offence had been committed and the court actually passed on the offence charged, the Government might interfere and rescind the order of the board?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but if an offence had been committed, while it existed the offence would still be intact and punishable. After the recision, then no one, by violating the order, could commit an offence. The Government might, of course, rescind an order of the board. As I say, the Government is not going to do so except on the principles it has followed in connection with the Railway Commission, and that policy has proved in the interest of the country and it should so prove here.
The distinction is so subtle that, I think, the minister has used his finest ingenuity on it.
Will the Government not interfere after an order has been given by the court?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The order is given by the Board of Commerce.
When the court has rendered its judgment and made a rule for enforcement, could the Government interfere?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Government could not interfere with the court. The case the hon. member brought to my attention was that of an order. An offence having been brought to the attention of the Attorney General and the court having decided that the offence had been committed, any interference on the part of the Government after the man had committed the offence, could not affect the matter .at all.

Clause 41 says:
The Governor in Council may, in His discretion, either upon petition of any person interested, lodged within one month after the making of the order, decision, rule or regulation, or within 'such further time as the board under special circumstances may allow, or of His own motion, at any time, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board.-*
But during that month, there may have been an order or a decision of the Superior or Exchequer court. What effect would the interference of the Government have with respect to that order?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Once a reversal was made of an order, then no further proceedings could be taken on that order; or if an order was varied, except in accordance with the variations.
Would it stop the proceedings already taken?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, proceedings already taken are taken.

The proceedings could be taken and not completed. For instance, if there is an execution in the Superior court against goods or valuables of the firm or corporation, would the interference of the Government prevent that execution from being carried out? Would it stop the proceedings?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the execution could go on because the execution could not have started unless proceedings in regard to the offence were started in the court. When th6 offence is once established, that goes through; the man- is guilty and he has to pay the penalty.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 42-rules of procedure:
This should form a subclause of clause 26. It seems to be a repetition.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I -will let this clause stand in the meantime and see if we can follow the hon. member's suggestion which seems to be a good one.

On section 44-services of process:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is there anything in the Bill making officials of other courts officials of this court. For instance, will the sheriff of a county or an official of the Supreme Court of Ontario be officials of this board?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, but in carrying out their duties as officials of their own court, they are really executing the orders of this board, because the orders of this board are made rules of their court.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The sheriff of a county is, I think, an official of the Exchequer Court.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then he would be at their disposal because any order can be made a rule of the Exchequer Court, and all the officers would be empowered to carry it out.

I notice that service may be made-:	_
By mailing by registered letters, postage prepaid, addressed to the. president, managing director and secretary at the head office or chief place of business of said company.
Supposing that head office is in the United States, and there is a local or branch office in Canada, would it not be. sufficient if this notice were addressed to the local office in Canada rather than to the head office if the latter be situated outside of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That might be the better way, but I think that is provided for in the latter part of paragraph (b).

Paragraph (b) says:
Provided that if in any case within the jurisdiction of the board it shall be made to appear to the satisfaction of the board, that service cannot conveniently be made in the manner above provided,-
The board may then summon by newspaper, but that, I think, scarcely covers the objection I have raised. For example, if the head office happened to be in India, at Bombay, or in South Africa, at Cape Town, why should the board have to wait two months when notice could be served on the local office of the company?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the Act as drafted is right, but it is not printed quite right. If the word " provided "-and I move this amendment-is placed out in line with the extreme left hand line of the page and thus made applicable to both (a) and (b) that will take care of the situation, because the board can effect service merely by publication both in the case of incorporated companies and in the case of partnerships and firms.	,
I think that would improve it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am very strong on the question of service. I do not like to have anybody put in jeopardy through not being served. I am not satisfied with this registered letter business, because I am afraid there might be a miscarriage of justice very often. I think there should be personal service, through a representative, every time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, if possible.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 47-costs:
I notice that the costs of and incidental to any proceeding before the board may be taxed. Taxed by whom?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would be covered by the general regulations which the board is empowered to make.

If a private individual makes a Complaint which does not result in a conviction, will he have to pay
the costs?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Not unless he was assessed with the costs by the board. If he acted bona fide throughout, no doubt the board would not assess him for the costs.
Air. AIcKENZIE: Is the prosecution at the instance of the Crown by So-and-so?
Air. A1EIGHEN: Oh, no.
Mr. AIcKENZIE: Is it a private action every time?	[DOT]
Air. A1EIGHEN: The prosecution is by the Crown, when it gets to the stage of prosecution. If the board comes to the conclusion that an individual has offended against an order of the board and submits the case to the Attorney General, prosecution proceeds through the regular court channels. ing to -conviction if an offence has been committed and to an order.
Mr. MeKENZIE: When a summons goes out for a man against whom a complaint has been laid to appear before the board,- in whose name does that summons go out? speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The public institution, as my hon. friend calls it, or the board-, is empowered, without revealing the name of its informant at all, to order Smith to appear. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If he has acted mala fide he would likely 'be assessed, but that is in the discretion of the board under section 47.

He is taking
chances.

a complaint should employ counsel and carry on the prosecution.

speechtext: Of a combine. That can be done, but the -board is empowered to act even under that Bill without any individual taking the responsibility.

speechtext: Section agreed to.

speechtext: I wish to say that the suggestion of the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Mowat) was really better, but to adopt it would require renumbering all the sections, and it would have no different effect from the present; so I think we had better Jet it stand as it is.

when the rules and regulations governing the board are drawn, care should be taken that the board shall have the right to go into any office and seize the papers or take precautions that they shall not 'be disposed of. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The suggestion is no doubt good and will be acted upon. As to section 19, which has been allowed to stand, the chairman takes the view that we cannot fix the salaries by this Bill. speechtext:

speechtext:
In subsection 2, the

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do you not think that clause 7 is contradictory? It says that when it is -found that a commissioner is interested, the Governor in Council appoints another man in his place. Then we put in a proviso at the end saying that he Is not disqualified.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is in the event of the Governor in Council not having taken action. There is a similar provision in the Railway Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I think you will search in vain in any of the higher courts for any such language. The minister is quite well aware of the extreme sensitiveness of the common law on this point.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is exactly section 13
of the Railway Act-	i

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That may be, 'but I am not familiar with the Railway Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
-and after thinking it over and discussing it with	some
others, including the Prime	Minister, they seemed _ to think it would be dangerous to take that proviso out-that there would be cases where perhaps great inconvenience would occur.
