COMBINES, MONOPOLIES TRUSTS AND ,	MERGERS.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Meighen, Bill No. 167, concerning the Investigation and Restraint of Combines, Monopolies, Trusts and Mergers, and the Withholding and Enhancement of the Price of Cbmmodities, was read the second time, and the House .went into Cbmmittee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the 'Chair.
k On clause 2-definitions. " Combine.":
. Mr. McKENZIE:	Perhaps the work of
the committee might be abbreviated by the minister stating wherein this Bill differs from the old Combines Act or is it practically the same?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, it is very different. I think, however, the committee already has a pretty full idea of the intent and scope of this measure from the discussion in a previous Act. I direct the attention of the committee to the clause:
The expression " combine " is used in this Act with intended relation to articles of commerce, and it shall be deemed to have reference only to such combines, immediately hereinafter defined, as, with relation as aforesaid; have, in the opinion of The Board of Commerce of Canada (or of a single member thereof acting under authority of and for the purposes of section eight of this Act) operated, or are likely to operate, to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, consumers, producers or others, and, limited' as aforesaid, the said expression as used in this Act shall be deemed to include,-
(a) mergers, trusts and monopolies, so called,-
That is to say, the scope of the operations of this board as affecting combines shall be directed against such combines as are detrimental to the public interest. In other .words, this Act recognizes the fact that there may be combines, and there may be purposes of combines, that are in full accord with the public interest, in the interest of the country. For example, combinations of capital, and of combinations for the purpose of working together towards increasing export trade. The greater our export

trade the better for the country. That is a good, laudable practice and a good reason for amalgamation, because there are times when it can. be better secured, indeed almost always, by that means. But if that same combination operates for the- purpose of keeping down the wages of its employees, combines for that purpose, or for the purpose of putting up the cost to its consumers, above what is reasonable to those purchasers, that is detrimental to the interests of the public, and for so doing a combine comes within the operations of the Act and is answerable to this board. Now, Part I of this Bill deals wholly with the duty of the board in relation to combines, mergers and combinations so called. Part II deals with the duty of the board in relation to unfair prices and unfair practices. The Bill is divided into those two parts, and such is the scope of each part.
Would the minister explain what he means by the words "or are likely to operate?" Are the board given divine insight?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, but there may be evidence that the purpose of a certain Act, or even a certain combination itself, is to operate against the public interest, which may be set out, for example, in communications that pass between the various bodies that are about to combine, and though no harm may be done there may be ample evidence that harm is intended, and the board is empowered to anticipate and prevent such harm.
Would the board be empowered to investigate the watered stock, or so-called watered stock, of companies, and determine the rate of return on the actual investment?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In respect to such companies as come within the scope of the Act, it would.

What is the reason for limiting the operations of this Bill to articles of commerce? There may be combines of various professions. For instance, there may be a combine amongst doctors, or amongst lawyers, or amongst dentists, that might be detrimental to the interests of the public. If the public, cannot obtain the services of these men at reasonable cost, combines of that kind would be detrimental to the public interest. In that event, why not include them under the operation of this Bill?	'
fMr. Meighen.]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, a Board of Commerce is a Board of Commerce, and we have to deal with the first offenders first.
I do not know that. There is a possibility that those who deal in commerce may not be the first offenders.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I rather think the demand of the country at the present time is to .deal with them first. The country, of course, may be deceived, but we will find that out.
Section 2-Definitions-"Combines". Expression to include Mergers, Trusts, etc. Control over business of others. Contracts, agreements, arrangements or combinations. "Combine" not to apply to workmen or employees. "Minister", "Board".

Would subsection (c) as to the fixing of a common price or a re-sale price apply to companies who fix the resale price of their goods? I understand that the Ford Motor Company, for example, fix the prices of their automobiles to their agents and customers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

They would be breaking
this law if they continued the practice?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is it not a common custom all over the world for certain manufacturers to fix the retail prices of certain commodities.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know how common it is, but if it is done, that operation may be reviewed by the board.
Would it not improve subclause (b) to add after the word "person" in both places where it appears the words "firm or corporation"?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Interpretation Act covers that. It defines person to include firm or corporation.

Do I understand that the fixing of a retail price might be investigated by the board, and that if it were not found to be detrimental to the consumer or to the public interest a person would still be allowed to continue the practice?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I presume so, if it was not detrimental to the public interest or unfair to the consumer. The actual fixing of prices would not be wrong merely in itself.

I think great difficulty
will be found in enforcing the clause re-

garding the fixing of a common price. On large numbers of commodities the price is fixed by the manufacturer, for instance, on patented articles, and the price in that case may or may not show a large percentage of profit in the transaction, but in many instances there is reason for a larger percentage of profit than on the staple lines of merchandise. In advertising and placing an article of that kind on the market the inventor incurs a very large initial expenditure, and he must recoup himself from the [DOT]sale of the article, and consequently he must get more than the ordinary rate of profit. They have a similar law in the United States, and I know they have found great difficulty in working it out. It has entailed serious hardship on many lines of merchandise such as I have referred to. Newspapers and magazines fix their selling prices. How are you going to deal with that practice?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have just stated that the fixing of the price itself is not an offence, but should the board find that it is fixed too high and is unfair to the consumer, they can issue a prohibition; but if they find the price is fair, they do not enjoin against it. One office of this Act is to put the imprimatur of the board upon a practice which is odinarily unfavourably looked upon, but which the board may find in actual fact to be in the public interest In a word, the fixing of prices will not be '*condemned as wrong merely because it is a fixing of prices, unless the prices are unfairly fixed.
I think the clause would apply equally well if that section were omitted. It is absolutely unnecessary.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

Because you reserve the right to interfere in any case, whether the price is fixed or not fixed. Fot instance, books are published at a fixed price and subsequently they are sold at a lower price, and the same remark applies to many other things that one. cannot think of at the moment, and the cla'use it seems to me is not necessary. It has a deterrent effect, but it does not help the section at all, which would apply just as well without it, because the board reserves the right to investigate without that provision.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it is necessary and fair. It is questionable if the fixing of prices as carried on is not criminal under the code. But this is designed to divide
the sheep .from the goats,-to ascertain where a fixed price is unfair and where it is not, and to leave alone the men who are all right and go after the others. There can be no complaint about giving the board power to do that.
But you legislate against fixing a common price?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, we do not.
There is no discretion given in the Bill.

If the hon. member will read in clause 2 a little higher up: "Have, in the opinion of the board operated, or are likely to operate, to the detriment of or against the interest of the public, consumers," etc., he will find then that this comes in as included there. I might just add, while speaking on this point, that the Committee in considering this generally during the last few weeks certainly felt that this particular clause should be retained.
Would the hon. member name some specific cases that came under the consideration of the committee?
I could give a number, but I do not wish to delay the committee.
One case, if you will, please.

I suppose this section would take care of the case of a producer selling his commodity to a trader with the distinct understanding that the price would not be lower than that fixed, and in the event of his selling at a lower price the producer would refuse to have further dealings with him?	,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. That operation is a combination or combine within- the meaning of this section, provided that the board find it is detrimental to the consumer in a particular case. They look into what is done in the particular case and they say: Now, because of the fixed prices they come within- the meaning of this sec- [DOT] tion, and we may deal with them if we find that the particular fixing of prices was detrimental to the public; but if we find it was not, we will not touch it.

We have a case in Montreal, where the Macdonald Tobacco company refuse to sell their goods to people to whom they take a certain dislike-they may not like the color of their hair. Would this Bill get after a company of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That, of course, is not touched on here, but there is a clause in part 2 of this Bill that covers the case. I would not like to say in advance whether it makes it compulsory on the man to sell to anybody. I would be glad to consider an amendment to that effect.

Take the case of a large concern' such as Swift and company with its headquarters Sn the United States. It dictates to butchers and meat dealers in Canada as to prices. Would this Bill reach a company of that kind? -

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly. We could prosecute their agents here.

I return to the point I raised before, Mr. Chairman, although it does not seem to impress the Acting Minister of Justice. There are firms in business that by the method of putting their goods before the public have a vested interest in a particular product, and they have a right to say, I think, what price should be obtained for .that product. In placing it in the hands of the retailer they fix the price at which that article must be retailed. Surely they have the right to determine the price that they should obtain for their product, especially if the public are willing to pay that price; I do not think it is fair that this board should interfere. For instance, a line of silks is widely advertised under a certain name by a certain, firm, and obtains prominence and standing in the community for class, quality, and so on. I do not think that the privilege of fixing the retail price of that commodity should he taken away from that firm under the operation of this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot express my amazement upon hearing the views of my hon. friend. For two sessions now he has been very declamatory about profiteering, and his appeals have really been so heartrending that at last we have yielded to him. Now he wants profiteering to go unchecked; any man, he says, should have the right to fix the price of his goods; he protests against any interference whatever. Why, he is the worst profiteer in preaching I have ever heard.
He protests only for Renfrew.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Just for Renfrew, yes.

I challenge the minister to point to one word that I have uttered during this or any other session by way of protest along the lines that he has sug-
[Mr. Jacobs.!
gested. An insane and hysterical cry against profiteering is going about the country at the present time, a cry which has no foundation in fact. The cases in point referred [DOT] to by the Chairman of the Cost of Living Committee the other day show that he does not know whereof he speaks, or that he has not obtained the information he should have obtained when the -witnesses were before him for examination. He referred to evidence given by a witness before the committee who stated that a certain line of merchandise, the manufacture of which cost $4.37^ a dozen was handed out to the consumer at 75 cents for each article; and he cited this as a case of profiteering. Evidently he is ignorant of the avenues through which a line of merchandise must pass before it reaches the consumer; otherwise he would not have stated that profiteering obtained in that case. That line of goods would not be sold direct to the consumer, or even to the retailer; it would be sold to the wholesaler. The Cost of Living Committee should have obtained from that witness further evidence as to the various stages through which that article passed before it reached the consumer. For instance, it goes from the manufacturer to the wholesale house. Any one who knows anything about the wholesale business knows that an article which cost $4,371 a dozen to manufacture could not be handled by a wholesale firm and sold at a fair profit at less than $6 or $6.50 a dozen. Then, when the article is put into the hands of the retailer, the Tetailer must pay freight, packing charges and so on, and he could not possibly sell the articles at less than 75 cents and still make a legitimate profit. Yet it is alleged that this is an item in connection with which profiteering obtkined. Futther, the same witness gave' evidence that a line of goods which cost $10.50 a dozen was sold at $2.50 for each article. That witness should have been able to tell the committee of the avenues-through which that particular line of merchandise passed before it reached the consumer. But the information left the Cost of Living Committee in that way and the impression was given that 'the spread was a large one between the cost of production and the ultimate cost to the consumer. We are not informed what price was obtained by the wholesale house to which that line of goods was sold by the manufacturer; consequently, an unfair impression has been left on the minds of the public, and for this the Cost of Living Committee is responsible. The same may be said of boots and shoes. Evidence was

elicited from a retail boot and shoe man who appeared before the committee that on a certain line of boots he obtained 50 per cent profit. Any one who knows anything about retail merchandising knows that if a merchant buys fancy boots at $12 and advertises them at $18 he is not attempting to obtain any too much profit, for rarely is it possible to sell the whole of a line of merchandise like that at the larger price; the dealer has to sell many of those boots and shoes at $15, $12, or possibly even for less than he paid for them. So that the statement which has been issued is not borne out by an actual calculation of the results in a year's transaction. If I remember correctly, the business of that witness amounted to a turnover of $51,000 a year on a capital of $16,000. The impression was given that he made 50 per cent profit on his entire turnover, but evidence was elicited from that man to show that his net profit on capital on the year's turnover was only 5.22 per cent. If he does not make a better return than that on his capital, he will be out of business in a very short time; for it is not enough to allow for losses, shrinkage in value of stock, and so on. But the point I make is that the impression has been allowed by the Cost of Living Committee to go abroad that the boot and shoe merchants and retail men have been making undue profits. I am sorry that I did not know that this Bill was coming up for discussion, because I have memoranda and data concerning a large number of similar items. 'However, I think I have said sufficient to show that the impression given out as a result of the investigations made by the Cost of Living Committee have had an unfavourable effect upon the minds of the public, and that this impression would have been created had the actual facts been obtained from the witnesses who appeared before that committee and had those who examined the nesses known how to go about the work that they had in hand. Some of the criticism that has been levelled against the Cost of Living Committee by the press has been justified, because the evidence was there if they had known how to obtain it, and they would have obtained it had they sufficiently posted themselves on the work that they had in hand and had dealt with it in a businesslike manner.

If the data the hon. member has and which he is so anxious to lay before the Committee is as reliable as the data which he has just given
to the Committee, I am sure that it will be exceedingly enlightening. If the hon. member had taken nearly as much trouble to follow the evidence taken by the committee as he has done to follow the press report, he might have been a little better informed.
The House has not had the evidence placed before it.

I will just take up the two cases specifically. The hon. member stated that the Chairman of the committee used' these figures on the floor of the House to show cases of profiteering, stating that a line of goods produced in 1914 at a cost of $4,374 per dozen and sold to the consuming public at the rate of $9 per dozen was evidence of a case of profiteering. The hon. member cannot find in anything the Chairman of the committee has said anything that will bear out that statement. What the Chairman of the committee said was that the fact that goods produced in 1914 at $4,374 per dozen, reaching the consumer at $9 a dozen, or a difference of 100 per cent, and produced in 1919 at $10.50 per dozen, reaching the consumer at $30 a dozen, or a difference of 250 per cent, was an evidence of profiteering. If the hon. member will take the pains to get the evidence-and it is available, all he has to do is to ask the clerk of the committee-he will'find that the witness who gave that evidence was questioned closely as to all the channels through which those goods passed. The hon. member states that the committee gave out evidence that was misleading with regard to profits made by a certain company that had a capital of $16,000 and that sold boots at a profit of 50 per cent. The committee gave out no such evidence. The committee got accurately the detailed evidence as to all the channels through which these goods passed, the cost of doing business, the gross and the net profits, and neither the chairman nor any member of the committee has made any statement that the profits made by this retailer of shoes were either just or unjust. The hon. gentleman is carried off his feet by statements made in the press. If he will just take the pains to get the actual facts, he will find that the committee got a little more accurate information than he has taken the trouble to obtain.
* Mr. PEDLOW:	I have taken all pains
possible to obtain the evidence adduced before the Cost of Living Committee, but without success. The evidence is not today printed and distributed. That evidence should have been printed and distributed

amongst the members of this House from day to day so that they would not have to rely upon press reports. The reporters have informed me that the press reports are absolutely correct in every particular.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: What is the effect of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: The other evening when we passed the Railway Act I said I would introduce a special Bill, which would embody clause 374 of that Act, and would also strike out the words " including compensation if any " in the telephone clause. I am now asking the House to pass a special Bill so that the matter may go before the Senate again in this way, and peftiaps they will reconsider their decision reached in connection with the Railway Act.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: What does this deal with?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: Just the power clause.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: At the time the matter was last before the House the minister and myself had one view and the majority of the House had a different view. Which of those two views is given expression in this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: I am embodying in this Bill the view of the House in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Mowat), and which refers only to the power question.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: I desire to say, with all due respect to the wish of the House and the majority, that I regard the step taken as a great breach of' faith with an established interest in this country. I care nothing about the particular company concerned, and I do not know anything about them. But this is a breach of faith, and if passed by both Houses it will do infinite harm to the public credit of Canada.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
If I remember rightly, this is a Bill brought by the minister against the views of the minister himself.

The last time this question came before the House, the question was whether or not we should confiscate certain property belonging to the Toronto and Niagara Poyrer Company. Is it the object of this clause to curtail the rights which were granted that company by this House in 1992?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: When the Bill came from the Senate there was an amendment to subsection 5, section 374, with reference to the power question. The Bill was referred to a special committee which made a report hack to this House agreeing to the amendment as it came from the Senate. When it was before this House the member for Parkdale moved an amendment to the clause. The amendment by this House was then sent on to the Senate and they refused to concur. In taking .clause 374 oht of the Bill I promised to introduce a special Bill that would embody the clause as passed by this' House, and we could then fight the matter out entirely on the one subject. I think that what the hon. member (Mr. Bureau) refers to is the fact that the other evening I suggested a different amendment. I stated that if the House did not agree to the amendment proposed by the member for Parkdale I was prepared to move one to provide that if the municipality should refuse to allow the company to enter, the matter could be referred to the Board of Railway Commissioners who should have the power to decide whether the company should have the right to enter the municipality or not. However, as the (Bouse refused to consider that amendinent, I feel I am in duty bound to present this Bill containing the clause as it was passed by this House in the Railway Act.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: This proposed legislation is the same as that which was carried on thg other night by a poor vote with a sparse house. I do not see any sense in sending that same thing back to the Senate, when they refuse to change their views. If the minister included the amendment he proposed the other night there might be some reasonableness in sending it back. But to send it back as it was, with clauses 5 and 6 just as moved; by the member for Parkdale and carried in a committee of this House by a vote of 56 to 52 or something like that, hardly a majority in a small house, we are just wasting our time.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: If the House wishes to continue the effort to remedy the grievance of the people in Ontario as well as that which might be felt by other provinces, I think we should persist in bringing before the Senate as often as we can a Bill in connection with this matter, and perhaps in time the remedy might be effected. There is every possibility that the clause as it is in the Bill now will not be concurred in by the Senate in view of their refusal even after the conference. But it is my bounden duty to submit the Bill, and the House can amend it in any way it sees fit. If the House thinks it should be sent to the Senate in a different form I am willing to consider any amendment.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
When the Bill containing this clause came before the House it was submitted to a sub-committee for special study and the committee made a report. The clause as approved by the Senate was that recommended by the sub-committee. As stated by my friend from Pontiac (Mr. . Cahill), when the Bill came before the House it was the old fight of the Toronto people against the Toronto Power Company. I objected to that, and one of my reasons was this: If the Toronto people have any grievance against a particular corporation on the plea that the Dominion Parliament has granted to it excessive powers and now want to diminish those powers, let them come before Parliament in the ordinary way and we will have a fight on the straight issues involved in this Bill. There is nothing to prevent any citizen of Toronto advertising the fact that he intends, with that object in view, to ask amendments to the charter of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company granted in 1902. Then we shall know where we stand. But I for one will not in any way acquiesce in the insertion of a provision in the general law affecting the railways of Canada in order to meet the views of a particular clique in Toronto or anywhere else. Let the Toronto people pursue the course I have suggested and not endeavour to accomplish their purpose by slipping into the general railway law an amendment which simply affects this particular company. But the advocates of the city of Toronto raise the cry that the rights of the municipalities are jeopardized unless we accede to their wishes. That is simply throwing dust in the eyes of the people. No such rights are jeopardized as is claimed. The fact is that a fight is being waged between the HydroElectric Commission and this particular company. Now I was one of the members of the Committee that granted the charter to the Toronto and Niagara Company in 1902, and so far I have seen no reason to recede from the position which I then took.



But I think it is unfair, however, to detain members of Parliament here at this stage for the purpose simply of inserting in a general Act a provision which has relation only to a fight between the Toronto and Niagara Company and the Hydro-Electric Commission. Such a principle is absolutely wrong. I do not believe it to be the function of this Parliament to serve the interests of any body of men or any clique, nor to interfere with 'the powers granted in a special Act by making an amendment to the-general law. If powers of too wide a character have been granted to this company, let them be attacked in the ordinary way, but do not seek by means of a measure such as this to accomplish that object. . It is said this company is encroaching upon the autonomy of the municipalities. We do not permit that in the province of Quebec. If an electric or power company sought to ransack our streets in order to promote their enterprises, our municipalities would say: "You will not get any patronage from us; we never encourage those who want to make themselves a nuisance in our midst. More than that, we have by-laws that provide against such nuisances." I think I can detect the kernel of the whole question. The HydroElectric Commission is under the control of the Provincial Government, and the latter has limited the freedom of the municipalities by compelling them,, when an outside company is desirous of entering upon their streets, to submit the necessary by-laws to the Lieutenant Governor in Council for approval. In that way, the Provincial Government, or the Provincial Legislature, have restricted the absolute control which an Ontario municipality should have over its own streets. If such legislation as that were introduced' into the legislature of the province to which I belong, I would oppose it to the utmost of my power. It is an encroachment upon the basic principle of municipal administration. The provincial authorities virtually say to the municipalities, and at the dictation of Sir Adam Beck, "We are going to take from you your rights in this matter, and if you want anything done in the way of transmitting electric energy you must go to the Lieutenant Governor in Council for permission." What does that mean? That means obtaining the consent of the Hydro- Electric Commission, behind which stands Sir Adam Beck. T ask those who say that we, by our legislation of 1902, have encroached upon the rights of the municipalities, to bear that in mind.

I was talking a few minutes ago about the effect that such legislation as is now proposed will have upon the credit of Canada. I say that such legislation is immoral, and I use the term advisedly. In 1902 the members of the House of Commons, and of the Railway Committee, were just as intelligent as hon. gentlemen who are members of the House and of the committee to-day. After hearing all the parties connected with the undertaking it was decided to grant the powers asked for, and there were good reasons for adopting that course. The committee who dealt with the Consolidated Railway Act heard Mr. Beck state the position of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company-not Sir Adam Beck, but Mr. Beck, of New York, who represented the bondholders of the company. What did he say? He declared that the powers granted to this company were granted' at a time when it was looked upon as an adventurous undertaking. They did not know whether they would succeed or not, they were ignorant of the extent of the outlay that would be involved, and people at that time were very reluctant to put their money into such enterprises unless there were special inducements that would tend to make the enterprise a commercial success. The application of the laws of electricity was in an experimental stage. No great transmission lines existed at that time-in fact, the only one then in operation was to be found in the riding which I have the honour to represent. It was the first long-transmission line that was ever built, covering a distance of twenty-three miles.
They were willing to risk their capital, and they had to induce others to risk their capital for that purpose; therefore they had to get wide powers and great advantages to secure the necessary financial strength. We granted those powers to them. Experiments have been made, and to-day we have found the way to transmit electricity, and are harnessing every power that can be harnessed in Canada. The province of Ontario have decided-and I have no criticism to offer, because it does not concern me; what concerns me is the honour and credit of this Parliament-to establish a system of electric power to be developed, distributed, controlled and handled by the province. They find they have a competitor in the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, and they want to have an advantage over this competitor by saying: We shall have the control of streets, alleys and public squares in the province of Ontario to

extend our lines, but you shall not. Now, this proposition was made, and it was answered immediately. It was asked: Why not go and submit your plans to the Railway Commission? Here is the answer of my hon. friends, the Acting Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways. We had the Canadian National Railway Bill before this House, and I objected to the expropriation powers, because all the Canadian National Railway Company had to do was to deposit their plans signed by a surveyor, and immediately title vested in the Crown. They said: If we were to file those plans with the Railway Commission, what would be the consequence? Immediately people would rush to those lands, buy them, and we would have to pay a higher price. That is the answer to this thing. Immediately the Toronto *and' Niagara Power Company deposit its plans the Hydro Electrie will go to work and establish their lines on the very territory which the private company cover on the plans it deposits.
I know that the position I am taking to-night is not popular-with the element in Ontario; let me qualify it in that way. I have received requests from friends of mine in Toronto, saying: Of course, you do hot belong to our province, and this is a matter for us; say nothing about this Bill, swallow it, let the clause go through. Before rendering service to my friends- and if there is a man willing to go the limit I am so far as I am only personally concerned-before rendering service to my friends in my personal capacity, as a member of this House representing this country I want first to see that I do not hurt my country's reputation and the reputation of this House. I know that all the Toronto papers are going to say I must have been bought up by somebody. Well, I will ask, them this time to abstain if they do not want to be guilty of a falsehood, and I would say to them: Do not measure Jacques Bureau's robe by your own yardstick. He is not on the market and does not sell.,
I am speaking from a sense of honour, a sense of conviction, and I say that we cannot fool in this House. We have had these clauses in the general Railway Bill time and again before the House, we have had them for three years running, and they have always been held up. Why? Because this purpose of trying to take away the rights of the Toronto and Niagara Power *company could not be served by this public legislation, and therefore it could not go through. To-day the general Railway
290J
Bill is through. Why should we bow down to any set of men who have any particular interest in any particular thing? I say no. The credit of this country is pledged to the fact that when it passes legislation, if the legislation is wrong, or if conditions have changed in any way so it requires amendment, special legislation shall be passed, and there shall be no attempt to put in public legislation such terms as will affect private legislation to serve the interests of certain individuals-interests which are not for the benefit of Canada, but for the benefit of a few.
It may be, Mr. Chairman, that this was not the view taken by a majority of the members of this House when they voted on it because they were not directly interested. It is just like the case of any sentimental or any emotional question you put up. I might cite prohibition. Your prohibitionists are very active and are willing to do anything they can. They will pass the plate at any meeting to encourage the other fellow to talk prohibition. But you will not see that with the anti. He is satisfied with the way things are going, he thinks that individual liberty ought not to he infringed, and assumes that every man thinks as he does. It is the same here. Those who are against this Bill are very active. I have been flooded with letters, I have received numerous telegrams, I have had interviews with personal friends asking me to abstain because it did not concern the province of Quebec. But, 'Sir, it concerns the Dominion of Canada, it concerns the Parliament of Canada, it concerns every ma'n who sits in Parliament, and it concerns every elector who sends him here. What are you going to do? Are you going to tell the people who got this charter: We are going to take it away because you are coming in the way of Sir Adam Beck or the Hydro Electric? I say, no.
' Sir SAM HUGHES: Would the hon. member kindly explain what the effect of these clauses may be?

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
The effect of them is to restrain certain powers which were granted to the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. I say that if you restrict those clauses without calling those people here to dieuss their charter and show what the conditions were when it was granted, you are not doing the right thing. My hon. friend who puts this question to me was in the House, he was in the Railway Committee when that charter was granted in 1902, and heard the argument

which then took place. Nothing has come to light since then to give me any reason to change my views, or his views, except the fact, as I have stated-and I repeat it again-that a new baby was born, called the Hydro Electric, and one would think, according to those gentlemen, that every right and every power granted ought to give way to that new baby. It is a breach of faith. It is immoral to repudiate any right you have given, as it is immoral to repudiate your debts. It is not because you have power to do a thing that it follows when you do so that it is always moral and right. I for one, Mr. Chairman, do not [DOT]see why this legislation is introduced tonight. Here we are at the end of the session, we desire to prorogue to-morrow, we have important legislation in front of us in the Franchise Bill to provide for by-[DOT] elections, we have Estimates to look into, .and yet to please a certain number of men -who have never given us a valid reason, except that this Toronto and Niagara Power Company was coming in conflict with the Hydro Electric-we are asked to pass legislation to amend a law of 1902, which is in itself a private law, without giving a chance to the people who received the benefits and powers granted by it to come before us and explain their position. As I have said, it is only a very small question. There are many millionaires in Toronto. Let them put their hands in their pockets-let them pass the hat if they want to get money to advertise in the Canada Gazette and the various newspapers that they are going to present a Bill to amend Act So-and-so; that is, the Act of the Toronto $md Niagara Power Company, and in that way give these people a chance to come before the committee. Then if the House sees fit, after going through the regular procedure, to curtail any of these powers, I say, well and good. But I will not submit to this-to use public legislation to serve the purposes of a few men to establish, as I have stated and as I repeat, the immoral principle of repudiation and of throwing to the dogs vested rights which have been granted. I for one will vote against the Bill.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
When the Eailway Bill
was before the House on the question of the action that the House should take on the report from the conference that was held between the Senate and the House of Commons, the Minister of Eailways (Mr. J. D. Eeid) stated that the Government had decided that the Bill should be divided in order that the general Eailway Bill might 
be saved this session The Bill was divided; the general Eailway Act passed through the House with certain amendments and went to the Senate. It has now been approved by the Senate and will become law, so that good purpose has been accomplished; the Eailway Bill will go into effect when assented to by His Excellency. But the Minister of Eailways also stated at that time, as also did the Prime Minister, that a Separate Bill would be introduced to cover the power portion of the legislation which was embodied in the general Eailway Bill and that it would be submitted to the House in order that it, too, might be sent up to the Senate.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
Is this a Government
Bill?.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: Of course it is a Government Bill, introduced by the Minister of Eailways.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
The minister knows that
scarcely a member of the Cabinet is in favour of this legislation. Why is it brought in at this time?

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: ' I can tell my hon. friend why it is brought in: because the Government, in order to save the general railway legislation from failure, considered that it was essential to divide the Bill, and gave promise on that occasion that a separate Bill would be introduced to deal with this matter.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: That they do not believe in.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: The Government are doing what they believe to be right in introducing this Bill and thus respecting the judgment of the House.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
Suppose this Bill
does not pass, will the general railway legislation, when assented to by the Governor General, stand as it is on the statute-book?

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
The general railway legislation will stand as it is. The Government have introduced it in the form in which it passed the House as part of the Eailway Bill. The Government simply divided the Eailway Bill into two sections; they put in the Eailway Bill all that related exclusively to railways, and they took out of it that which related to power. Now they submit to the House the power clause in the form in which this House passed it; and I submit that the Government is doing right in respecting the judgment of the House.

457T
The House expressed its opinion in the matter and the Government are carrying out what the Prime 'Minister promised last week when the Bill was before the House-that the Government would submit a Bill carrying out the decision of the House as embodied in the Railway Bill.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: Against the report of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: Because the House overruled the report of the committee. If the House had decided in some other way, then the Government would have submitted the Bill in a form which would be in accordance with the decision of the House.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: By a majority of four, too. There were very few in the House.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
I myself was in the
minority on that occasion.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: It was smuggled through.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: It is the duty of the Government to submit to the House what the House itself decided and to act in accord' ance with what the Prime Minister and the Minister of Railways stated to the House.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: When did the Prime Minister or any one else in authority present this Bill to the House and state that it would be passed? This is. not what I understood would be brought in; this is not the kind of legislation that I understood the Prime Minister promised.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: It is what I understood the Prime Minister promised; that is all I can say.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
I was going to say that 1 voted against the Mowat amendment when formerly before the House for this reason: For two years the railway legislation had failed by reason of a conflict of opinion between the two Houses, the Senate having taken one view and this House having taken another. As the Minister of Railways intimated on that occasion, he believed, from the information he had, that the Senate would not accept the proposal embodied in the Mowat amendment, and that, quite apart from the merits of the proposal, it was inadvisable to risk the loss of the whole Bill by adopting that amendment. Personally, I would have been glad to support the amendment suggested by the Minister of Railways or the amendment suggested by the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), or the amendment suggested by the member for South Simcoe (Air Boys)
in the hope that the Senate, as a settlement of this long controversy, might accept the amendment. But the House did not adopt that course; the House took the other course and adopted the Mowat amendment; therefore this Bill is introduced to carry out what the House itself decided.
Just a word or two with reference to the remarks made by my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau). This is more than a local dispute, and whatever one's opinion may be on the merits of the dispute in Toronto, we must face the question in the light of the larger issue as to what control the Parliament of Canada or the public should have over power companies operating throughout Canada-because this company's charter is not limited to Toronto or to Ontario; it extends throughout the whole of Canada. Personally I am not concerned, I am not troubled about what took place when the Bill granting this charter was passed by this-House in 1902. I think it is quite clear from the record in Hansard that at the time it was passed nobody thought the Bill gave the company the powers which the Privy Council has decided that the company has. But I am not basing any view that I entertained upon what took place then, I entertain . this view-and I think it is the fair view-that no company, no matter what its charter rights may be, should be permitted, under the conditions prevailing to-day, to enter upon the streets of any city at its own sweet will, uncontrolled by any power, government or municipal.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
But if the Parliament of
Canada gave them the authority to do so?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
Just as the Parliament
of Canada originally gave the railways the authority to do certain things and afterwards appointed the Board of Railway Commissioners to regulate and control those railways, thereby regulating and limiting the exercise of their charter rights, so I believe that Parliament is entitled to regulate and limit, in the public interest, the exercise of the charter rights of any power company.
, Mr. JACOBS:	Not without compensation.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
If an agreement were reached between the House of Commons ,and the Senate along the lines of the amendment suggested by the Minister of1 Railways or the amendment suggested by the member for Shelburne and Queen's, then you would be regulating the rights and powers of this company, you would

not be confiscating them, but you would at the same time be protecting the municipalities and conserving the public interest. Under such an amendment this company could not enter upon the streets of the cities or towns in any part of Canada .without the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners. We may assume that the board would only grant that privilege if	it	was	in the	public	interest,to	do	so.	I would	hope	that if
the House passes this Bill and it goes to the Senate, the Senate would see their way clear to end this controversy by a fair compromise that would protect the municipalities and at the same time would not confiscate the powers that may be necessary for the operations of the company. If the Senate would agree upon an amendment requiring that before a company could enter upon the streets of any city or town, the approval of the Board of Railway Commissioners should be secured and that the company could enter only under the terms and conditions provided in an order of the board, I believe that that would be a reasonable compromise as between the views of the Senate and the views of this House, and that this long controversy would be ended. I do think that the Minister of Railways was right in submitting the Bill to the House in the form in which he has submitted it, because the Prime Minister stated to the House that the intention was to divide the Railway Bill, send the Railway Bill, upon which the House and the Senate had agreed, up to the Senate in order that it might be put through, and submit the other relating* to power in the form approved by the House to the House in order that it might be dealt with by the House and the Senate.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
This matter appears to have originated about the year 1902. The hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) was a member of the House at that time, and he is no doubt familiar with the action taken by Parliament in 1902. It was felt that the Bill, as it passed the House in that year, protected the rights of the people throughout the Dominion. Members representing some of the western ridings took a great interest in the debate and tried to protect the rights of the various municipalities and were of the opinion that they had succeeded in doing so. Some years after the Bill passed the House, there was a fight between the city and the Niagara Power Company, and on the matter 
going to the Privy Council, 'the company discovered that they had greater rights than they understood they had when the Bill passed the House. On the basis of that, they apparently issued a large amount of stock, on which they are now claiming that there are vested rights.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: The assertion has been repeatedly made that the rights which were granted in 1902 were not fully understood by the company until a number of years later. What is that assertion of fact based upon?

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: Surely what developed after 1902, namely, the appeal to the Privy Council and the interpretation of the Act, is what they based their claim on.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: What was the decision of the Privy Council?

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
The company issued stock notwithstanding that interpretation, and now they claim vested rights. Surely the municipalities have vested rights just as much as this company has. Surely the hundreds of thousands of people who live in the various municipalities throughout the Dominion have vested rights in those municipalities. They are only asking that that company should come into the municipalities under the direction of a tribunal, but the company 9 p.m. says: No, we have a right to go in and do what we like, place unsightly poles on and take possession of the streets in your cities without any consideration as to what your cities may want. The hon. member stated that this measure passed the House with a small attendance of the members. I do not know what took place in 1907, but I think it carried with quite a large majority with a very good House. Surely the members of the House of 1917, which carried this Bill by a majority, had as much intelligence as is possessed by the House to-day and especially by some of those on the Opposition side who claim that they have exceptional intelligence in dealing with matters of this kind. The Bill also passed by a majority of those in attendance in this House in 1919, and surely that is an indication of the feeling of the representatives of the people. It comes back to this House, and we claim that it is no't only a Toronto matter, but one that affects all municipalities throughout the Dominion, from, east to west, and there are objections from large numbers of municipalities-I think, from 100 to 170 of them who, at a representative gathering a

short time ago, gave expression t-o their opposition. Surely the people representing those 100 to 170 municipalities know what they want, and they object to this company having those exceptional rights and claiming vested rights as against the vested, rights of the people of the municipalities. It is only a reasonable thing, when this Bill has passed this House of Commons twice by a majority, a fair expression of a majority, of those in attendance having been given, to expect that the members here to-night are not going to sit idly by and allow two or three members of the Opposition to get up and shout "vested rights," and then to say that they have no interest in this matter; that they are not fighting for the interest of vested rights. No doubt, they presume they are right, but the fight that some members are putting up in this matter suggests that there is something more than protecting vested rights. This is a company, that as I have said more than once, has a great influence with public representatives throughout the Dominion and also with parliaments. It seems that they have sufficient influence to come to this Parliament under any government and get almost what they like. Surely it is time that the people's rights were protected by their representatives. People's rights have -been protected by a vote of this House twice; but there is a shout to-night that this should be all changed for the benefit of vested rights of this corporation that is not confined to one or two branches but to many, and that, as I have said before, is the greatest exploiting company that was ever produced in Canada or, indeed, in America, and their hand has been shown to-day and has been shown continuously. Surely to-night we shall cease to show that an exploiting corporation is going to have this influence over members of the House and to prove that the vested rights of the people are going to be protected by a majority of the House.
-Mr. BUREAU: Do 1 understand the hon. member to say that the stand taken by certain members- on this side of the House creates a feeling in his mind that they have something more than tire public interest at heart, and that there is suspicion?

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: I have said that the very great interest some members are taking in these debates looks very suspicious, not only to 'myself but to many others. .

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
Will the hon. gentleman name the members and say what kind of
suspicion he has? He is a man of honour; he sits in this House, and if he is referring to any man in this House, I want him to give the name and to state what his suspicions are.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: I am not naming members.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: It is a gratuitous insult.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: It is my right to ask that of the hon. gentleman or that he take back his statement. T am one of the members of the Opposition, and if the hon. gentleman wants to point to any of my colleagues on this side, he ought to be manly enough to get up and name him. If he is not, he ought to be manly enough to get up and apologise.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: There is no apology forthcoming.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: And the hon. member has no names to give. Then the argument coming from that stamp of -man will not convince me nor any man of my brand.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: There is no hear, hear. A man who is going to suspect my motives must tell me why, and if he does not do so, I have a right to suspect the heart and mind of such a man, and I have a right to despise him. I do not belong to any clique nor to any band; I am an honest man; I stand here as such, and do not, want any man to cast any suspicion on my honesty or my honour, especially when he can only insinuate and then sit down and hide his face in shame; when he is not manly enough to get up and name those whom he wants to accuse, when he has no ground for his suspicion, but it is only a little bit of spite on his part to talk about protecting public interest. 1 pity the people who entrust their protection into the hands of men such as he is.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: He is a little overcome by the heat.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
It is not the heat that overcomes men who make such insinuations in this House. The heat is only skin deep, but these insinuations start from lower down and deeper than the skin. There is something below the skin and inside the carcass-that something which ought to be in every man, and which is called heart, but which cannot be found, any more than honour, in the member who has just spoken. He will not come down to facts, but deals in generalities. He says that the

municipalities have vested rights which must be protected. I say that his argument is just as good as the accusation he has just made.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: My hon. friend, I think, is exceeding the hounds of the rules of order in his remarks. There should of course be no insinuation made against the honour of any hon. member of this House.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: If the minister will take upon himself to have his supporters withdraw the nasty and low things they have said against us and apologize to us, I am willing to bow to his ruling, but if hon. gentlemen on one side of the House sling mud at hon. gentlemen on this side,, I for one am not going to stand for it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: It is for the Chair in both cases to direct what shall be the procedure of the House.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: I shall listen to the Chair and not to my hon. friend, and I shall go on as I like until the Chairman calls me to order. The hon. member (Mr. Thomas Foster), who used such sweet language, spoke of the vested rights of the municipalities. The municipalities have no vested rights in the province of Ontario so far as the Hydro-Electric is concerned.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: Have the municipalities no rights in the streets which they have laid down, .and paved? I am not talking about the Hydro, but about the municipalities.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: We are discussing the Hydro now. The municipalities ought to have unlimited and absolute rights, but before they can make any agreement respecting the transmission of power it has to be submitted to the Lieutenant Governoi of the Province, if I understand the law aright.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: I beg to correct the hon. gentleman. We are discussing the rights of municipalities, and not the Hydro.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
We are discussing the rights of municipalities as affected by this Bill, in respect to the transmission and distribution of power.
(Sir SAM HUGHES: Under the provincial law creating the Hydro-Electric Commission what rights have the municipalities as against the Hydro in the matter of poles, for instance? I say they have no rights.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
It has been frequently stated by Ontario members in this House,

by Ontario lawyers, that any agreement with regard to the transmission or distribution of power has to be submitted to the Lieutenant Governor for his approval. Is that right? Therefore I say they have no absolute rights, for those cannot be absolute rights which are subject to the approval of the Lieutenant Governor. The rights are restricted in that way. Furthermore, the amendment presented to the House by the Minister of Railways to-night is the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Parkdale, and there was never any understanding that that amendment should be accepted by the House. Therefore T beg to move to amend clause one by striking out subsections 5 arid 6 of the said clause and replacing same by the following subsections :
Any specific powers inconsistent with the provisions of this Act and conferred on any company by any special or other Act or authority of the Parliament of Canada or of any province shall not be affected by the provisions of this Act, but if any municipality complains to the board that any company whether incorporated by special or other ^Act or authority of the Parliament of Canada is exercising its powers oppressively or in bad faith the 'Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada may hear such complaint and if it sees fit supervise the exercise of such powers: Provided always that whenever any company incorporated by Special Act of the Parliament of Canada acquires the assets of a company operating within a municipality, which said municipality has the right by agreement to purchase any of the assets of such company, then and in every such case the municipality may enforce its rights under such agreement as fully as if such purchase had not been made, and may enforce against such purchaser the provisions of such agreement as if it were the original party entering into such agreement with the municipality.

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext: This Bill is not a fight, as my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) would fain make out for the interests of the city of Toronto, but a fight for the municipalities throughout Ontario and largely throughout the West. With reference to my hon. friend's statement regarding the amendment of the hon. member for Parkdale, that amendment was submitted to the House and was debated for a whole afternoon and the greater part of the evening; a vote was taken upon it, and the amendment was adopted in preference to any other amendment and in preference to the report of the committee to whom the Railway Act had been referred. So, when my hon. friend says that this Bill has been smuggled into the House, as I understood him to say-

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.
speechtext:
If I did not say it, I
meant it.

speechtext: Well, that is a very contracted and narrow view, and I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should entertain it. It is not a fight by the city of Toronto alone, by any means. It was the one nearest its grasp and a prize most earnestly desired. For that reason and owing to the unfortunate name which the incorporated company bears-the Toronto and Niagara Power Company-there has been charged to the city of Toronto and its representatives all the trouble that has accrued from the legislative measure passed by this House in 1902, which was not understood by the members of the House, and which I venture to say was as little understood by-the member for Three Rivers, who I believe was a member of the House then, as he understands the real situation regarding this matter to-day. I want to illustrate the .modus operandi of the company which the hon. gentleman is so earnestly defending. The Toronto Electric Light Company acquired originally a franchise

maintopic: BILL RESPECTING ELECTRIC AND POWER COMPANIES.

Well, I will say principle then. The justice of this Bill can stand absolutely upon its merits, when you consider broadly the influences which this Bill will exercise throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion, and particularly in Ontario. Originally we had in Toronto an incandescent light company which had a charter for the distribution and manufacture of electric light. This charter was acquired by the Toronto Electric Light Company which has distributing power for the distribution of light, heat and power in Toronto.
It produced its energy by steam-power. It was subsequently acquired by the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, which had constructed transmission lines to conduct power developed at Niagara Falls to the city of Toronto for the purpose of supplying the electric light company of Toronto and the Toronto 'Street Railway Company. For that original purpose the Toronto and Niagara Power Company got from the Federal 'Government a charter to issue bonds amounting to a million and a half dollars. It is important that we should consider why the Hydro-Electric Company in Ontario was developed. The Toronto and Niagara Power Company, or the Toronto Electric Light Company, which was a subsidiary, had the arbitrary and absolute power at that time to distribute light, heat and power in the city of Toronto and to exercise discrimination practically as they pleased. They said they would give power or would not give it as they saw fit, and every one knows what that means. Is there any manufacturer in this House who will not say that it is an advantage to a manufacturer to have electric power when his competitor has to operate his business by ordinary power developed by steam? For a time in the city of Toronto they held the manufacturers' interests in their hands and discriminated as they pleased. I happened to have for the city of Toronto at that time the operation of a large machine shop, where we manufactured our own carts and wagons, brushes and brooms, and was refused by them the introduction of electric power, and for a long time steam had to be used. To that extent the discriminating power rested in the hands of the Toronto Electric Light Company, and it was for such reasons as this that it became evident to the municipalities of Toronto and others that some opposition would have to be developed and that some other means would have to be provided in order to distribute light, heat and power, not only to the city

of Toronto, but to the various municipalities throughout Ontario, in order to get away from the grasping greed and controlling avarice of the company which at that time practically monopolized all power distributable anywhere near the Niagara Falls. After the matter was discussed the HydroElectric came into existence under splendid control and management and with the prestige and support of the Ontario Government, not simply to oppose this Power Company, but to give the people of Ontario the liberties to which they had a right, and to release the manufacturers from the ,bondage which otherwise they would have suffered under the influence of the controlling characteristics of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company and its subsidiaries. It is all very well to accuse Adam Beck of being avaricious and desiring to put this company out of business. This company never was menaced. The cry about bonds and vested rights is a bugaboo, nothing more nor less. They issued bonds to the extent of a million and a half.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals

My remarks will be
brief, and five minutes will suffice me for the purposed The Senate inserted an amendment into the Consolidated Railway Act to which a majority of this House would not agree. From the Senate it went to the special committee of the Commons who did concur in it. However, upon the
measure returning to this House, by a majority vote the members agreed to pass the amendment which is now in the present Bill. I suggested that if the amendment of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) did, not pass, I would have another amendment which perhaps the Senate might be induced, to agree to. However, the amendment of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Mowat) having been, resolved on, I had no alternative, I simply had to let the Bill go through. There is no doubt that the Senate will reject the amendment of the member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau), and I am also of opinion that the Senate will reject the provision in this Bill. The only question then is, will the House stand by its amendment and bring it forward from session to session until the situation is cleared and the difficulty removed, or would hon. gentlemen prefer to accept the amendment I intended to move, and which is to be found in Hansard? Would they prefer to send that to the Senate and see if the Upper Chamber would agree to it? I am not particularly wedded to the amendment contained in the Bill and if the House wishes to adopt any other form I am quite willing to agree and let it go forward to the Senate. Undoubtedly it would be a very important matter to the municipalities of the whole Dominion if the charter of this Company were to remain in force for all time. But I have already stated here my belief that before another session comes around that charter will be absorbed, probably by the Ontario Government, and the present difficulty will disappear. This charter will become null and void, and there is no other company in existence with any such extensive powers applicable to the whole of Canada. Therefore, I do not think the matter is such a serious one after all. What we should do is to reaffirm the stand we have already taken in this House. That is the only thing I am anxious to do, and, therefore, if we pass the Bill in its present form, or in the form it would be with the amendment I have in contemplation, I think we should be adopting a proper course. The Bill in its original form contained my amendment but I struck it out and inserted the amendment of the hon. member for Park-dale. I did that because it was intimated to me that otherwise my action might be misconstrued, and I might be accused of not acting fairly in the matter. Having stated the situation may I ask that we lose no more time but proceed to vote on the different amendments, and whatever decision

the House comes to will be promptly forwarded to the Senate for their adoption.

speechtext:
I would be exceedingly glad to have the question settled quickly if I was. quite sure we knew all about it. I think many matters have been imported into this discussion which might very properly have been left out as having nothing to do with the vital question before us. We are not concerned about the Toronto and Niagara Power Company-except for what has .been said in this House I do not know who they are; we are not concerned with regard to the relations between the Hydro-Electric and Sir Adam Beck and the Government of Ontario; they are not* considered in this matter at all. And I am, not concerned to insist that this is a Toronto matter, I am going to accept the view that it is a matter affecting all the municipalities of Canada because the Bill touches them all. I sympathize with the difficult position of the Minister of Railways. He undertook to bring down a certain Bill. Really what he undertook to do was to separate this' disputed matter from the other portions of the Railway Bill which were not disputed. But I did not understand that when he agreed to separate it and bring it forward! in a distinct Bill he was committing the House to what that Bill should be. I do not understand that we were bound by any previous decision of the House. Surely-my hon. friend must have meant, when he said he would bring the matter before the House for further .Consideration that it was for open consideration and for free debate. And it is worth while remembering thalt while the House did decide on a certain point-and I bow with great respect to the will of the House-it was not a majority; that is to say, it was a majority of half the House. It is quite possible- I have no reason 'to think it is so-that the House as constituted might have a different view. And it would have the right to have a different view; it is not bound by the decision reached at that particular time.
It seems to me 'that really the vital question is the matter of public faith. I think we are not concerned about this particular company, but I appeal to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to agree with me when I say that we are concerned to keep faith when we pledge ourselves to a charter in this way. I do not care,-if you like I will admit-that the charter granted in. 1902 was unwise and 'improvidenij, and.

that we would not grant it to-day. Nevertheless we granted that charter, and although it may have been improvident, although it may have been unwise, I say it we are going to proclaim to the wide world that a charter which the Parliament of Canada gave to a body of men, and on the faith of which they invested their money, is not to be respected by this Parliament, then we do a great wrong to the public of Canada. I do not care about the interests of the company, but I say that every man who has occasion to go to the money market of the world for a private enterprise, or a corporation enterprise, or a municipal enterprise, or a provincial enterprise, aye, or a Dominion enterprise, has an interest in seeing that tne public faith in charters granted by this Parliament shall not be destroyed. That is the question. Are we going to treat our charters as scraps of paper? What have we been fighting for over in Flanders and France? We have been fighting against the Prussianism which -tore up a treaty and said it was a "scrap of paper." Do not let us tear up charters which this Parliament of Canada grants. If we made a mistake, it is our fault; it is not the fault of the men who got the charter. At a time when credit, private and public, municipal, provincial and Dominion, is so important we should do nothing to impair it.
I beg the Parliament of. Canada, if this question is open to us to-day, to vote in such a way that we shall maintain the rights granted to a company by a solemn charter.
Mr. M'OWAT: I was the mover of this amendment, and I do not want to go over the same ground again. But I wish to point out, in answer to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) that the charter he speaks of as having been given, which he now says ought not to be treated as a " scrap of paper," ds exactly the reverse of what he describes. The charter we granted to this company was a charter which required that the consent of any municipality which the company wished to sell electricity to should be first secured. Nobody disputes this. By a mistake in drafting, when we came to 1903, that great protection of the municipalities was left out, and the company is now seeking as the result of a mistake to get more than we gave them. As a matter of fact, it is not Toronto that is interested in this company; it is Montreal. It is fair to say that my hon. friends opposite who come from Quebec, where Montreal is, are interested in opposing this thing, because Montreal money is risked in it. It is just as proper for us to make that charge as it is for hon. gentlemen opposite to say that it is the Toronto people who are interested. We must legislate on the merits' of each case that comes before us. Here an absolute mistake wras made, and we have the power to go back and correct it in favour of the public and to restore the rights that were, in this mistaken way, taken from the public. This contest involves far more than the rights of this particular company; it is a contest between the union of municipalities of Canada and interlocking companies. If you reverse the action taken by this House in 1917, and again last month, you strike a blow at municipal and public rights that will be regretted for many years. Strong arguments have been made by corporate interests against interference with what are called vested rights, but those arguments should not stand. It might be said that " vested rights" are not vested rights. In the case I mentioned of the mistake in the pay envelope, the procedure followed would not be that of saying: Oh, let this man alone; labour is scarce; we must not interfere; .keep the law off him. No; the law says that we must put a strong hand on anything which involves other than an honest intent; and it should be the same with this com-' pany.
