[Mr. Mowa.t.1
diction in connection with the regulation oi public service corporations. During my hon. friend's term of office in the Government of that day and during the term of office of subsequent Governments, legislation has been repeatedly passed in this House taking away from public service corporations rights and privileges which they enjoyed by virtue of their charters and by virtue of the common law. If a railway corporation is by its original charter granted the right to charge whatever rates it chooses for freight and passenger traffic, has the Government no right to step in and say: You shall charge a certain rate and you shall charge no more? When we do that we take away from the corporation the right to increase its earnings by taking a step which they were permitted to take under their original charter or at common law. We are not confiscating any of the rights of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company; what we wish to do is simply to pass legislation which will have the. effect of regulating the exercise and enjoyment of those rights. They had the power under their charter to sell and distribute electricity in this country in wholesale quantities. When they appealed to the Privy Council they ascertained that they enjoyed a right which was not anticipated when their charter was granted. The Government now say: We are not taking away your right to sell and distribute power to towns and villages in wholesale or retail quantities; we are imposing upon you a condition with which you must comply before' you exercise the rights which you received under your charter. It is simply a matter of the regulation of the manner In which they should carry on their business as a public utility throughout this Dominion.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

Just before the House
rose at six o'clock I called attention to certain matters that had been placed before the House by the Chairman of the Cost of Living Committee. He charged the retailers of this country with profiteering and when I so stated he said that it would be impossible for me to produce evidence of any such charge. I find on page 4450 of Hansard the following which I should like permission to read.

I am very sorry but I cannot allow the hon. member to read a single line of a speach which was delivered in another debate in the present session. It would be absolutely against the rules to permit it.
The hon. member challenged me to produce proof.
The hon. member can refer to the page number of Hansard if he so desires.

The proof of my statement will be found on page 4450 of Hansard. The Chairman of the Cost of Living Committee has received many compliments from the members of that committee, and I have no desire to detract from them in any way. The hon. member for East Algoma is undoubtedly full of enery and it

was evident to everyone of us, and especially to the members of his committee, that he worked hard and unceasingly in and out of season to produce results. But I contend that it was impossible for any good results to be obtained by that committee from its very composition. It was composed of fourteen members, three of whom were lawyers, two agents, three farmers, two publishers, one a merchant, one an educationist, one a broker, and one a lumberman^ The idea of appointing such a committee to investigate a commercial proposition seems to me ridiculous. You might as well appoint a committee of blacksmiths to investigate a case of malpractice on the part of a doctor, and the result of their deliberations would be just as effective. I notice in the report of that committee this admission: "Your Committee have not yet reached a point in their investigation that would warrant them in submitting final conclusions." Then the report immediately goes on to enunciate the conclusions the Committee have arrived at. The member for Shelburne and Queens and also the Chairman of the committee insisted that the publicity obtained by this Cost of Living Commission was of great value to the country. On the contrary, I think it has intensified the unrest that obtained prior to its appointment, and instead of allaying the suspicion which a great many people entertained it has only increased it. The Chairman of the committee held that if members of the House wanted to have information at first hand they should have the evidence, buit that evidence has never been circulated. At any rate, I have made many unsuccessful atterhpts to obtain copies of it. The O'Connor Report two years ago and the McFall Report subsequently if acted1 on by the Government would, I submit, have covered the situation just as effectively as the Bill before the House. I understand that only on two occasions lias there been any attempt to invoke the Act which was passed in 1910. That Act, as far as I can see, makes provision for the same purposes as the Act now before the House, and with the exception that one is a little more extensive in some respects, the machinery is much the same. If the Government had been sincere and not afraid to enforce the provisions of that Act they might have prevented a great deal of the difficulty that now exists. The report published by Dr. McFall and the particulars given therein are entirely misleading. For instance, that report says:

In many instances, -Canadian cloth for suitings and overcoats is going forward for sale at an eight to ten per cent -decrease. Apparently the middlemen are loaded with old stocks of the higher priced materials which they desire to sell to the public at the old prices.
The man who makes that statement may, he a learned doctor and all that sort of thing, but he has no knowledge of commercial conditions at the present time. A man occupying his position, a commissioner in the employment of the Government, should make sure of his facts before making a statement of that kind, which is so alarming, because such reports made without any attempt at thorough verification have an injurious effect. The hon. member for Red Deer speaking on this subject the other day put his finger on the right spot and I think that the Government would do well to heed his words and turn its investigations in the direction suggested. If the Minister of Finance would consult with the Minister of Customs- he would ascertain to a great extent the cause of the high cost of living. He would see that on merchandise imported into this country the customs tariff is, without question, to a large extent, responsible for high prices, and the present discontent. Members of the committee may doubt this statement, but I will submit one or two facts to show that the consumer pays the customs duty in every case, as well as the profit that is added. I have an advertisement taken from the Saturday Evening Post of an article of interest to the farmer and the mechanic alike. A brace and bit advertised for sale in the United States at $3.50, costs in Canada $5. The Canadian consumer pays that difference. Another item is a garden rake advertised in the same journal of another edition. The price in the United States is $1.50 and in Canada $2. The gardener in Canada has to pay the duty. Here is an item that is not of much interest to me, but may be to the Acting Minister of Justice. It is a Gem iSafety Razor. Those who are not so barefaced as the acting minister will have no use for this instrument of torture, but for the information of that hon. gentleman I will quote the price, which is $1 in the United -States and $1.50 in Canada. Then I see a fire extinguisher costing in the United States $10 and in Canada $12.50. I take these items promiscuously and not through any particular arrangement. Here is something of interest to every householder-Campbell's vegetable soup. It is also advertised in the Saturday Evening Posit and can be bought in the United -States at twelve cents a can, whereas 291
the householder in Canada must pay eighteen or twenty cents. This all goes to show who pays the duty. I want to emphasize this point, and I would like it to be emphasized in the press also, because it is very enlightening. The question is often asked: Who pays the duty? I think these illustrations show conclusively ' who does. The next item is Congoleum art rugs, the Canadian price being twenty-five per cent higher than that in the United -States. Then there is liquid cement, bought at 80 cents in the United States and $1 in Canada. For the Oliver typewriter the price is $57 in the United States and $72 in Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I submit that from these facts it will ibe easy for the Minister of Finance, as I indicated before, to consult with the Minister of Customs to decide what he and the Minister of Customs should do in order to remove or allay the dissatisfaction that prevails in this country at the present time. I also wish to place before the House some other facts in connection with the report on which this Bill is founded, and that is in regard to hosiery. From my own personal knowledge I know that the inference that has been drawn from the evidence submitted -to the committee on the cost of living is absolutely unfair. That is to say in the application of that evidence, as handed out to the public in general, there seems to be a disposition on the part of the investigators to place the onus and the responsibility on the retail trade of Canada. I submit, Sir, that that is neither correct nor fair. Take a line of ribbed wool hose that cost $2.25 per dozen in the year 1914-15 and sold retail at 25 cents per pair. The cost of those articles at the present time is $9 per dozen, and the retail price $1 per pair. Take a second lin-e: Worsted hose, cost $4.50 per dozen in 1914-15 and retailed at 50 -cents per pair; the same article to-day costs $12 per dozen and retails at $1.35 per pair. Take a third line: Fine wool hose. The cost of these in 1914-15 was $6.50 per dozen, and they retailed at 75 -cents per pair. The same line costs to-day $15 per dozen, and retails at $1.75 per pair. Take still another line of heavy worsted hose for boys' wear. The cost in [DOT]1914-15 was $8.50 per dozen, and they retailed at 85 cents per pair. The same line costs to-day $20 per dozen, and they retail at $2.25 or $2.50 per pair. This particular line can be bought in any retail store on Sparks street, Ottawa, at these prices. Then take another line of fine ribbed cashmere hosiery, manufactured in the city of Hamilton. This is a standard line and has been

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know what the political conscience of my hon. friend can

be like. I cannot understand, if he believes this legislation will be no good, why he does not oppose it? Much of his remarks I could not hear, but I understand he was comparing high prices in Canada with prices in the United States by reading a catalogue which I presume was his own. The attention of the board should be dravsm to the case of this store in Renfrew.

I desire to correct the
Acting Minister of Justice. I gave as my authority certain statements which I obtained from the Saturday Evening Post that no sane merchant living in Canada would attempt to advertise in. Those prices quoted are the prices paid by the consumer in the United States in the one case, and the other prices paid by the consumer living in Canada, in the other case, owing to the duty that prevails on the article in question.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 6-application to member of board for order directing an investigation:

I bwant to propose an amendment to this section-to Strike out the words "British subjects." The section will then read: "Any resident in Canada of full age" and so on. I cannot see why we should make any distinction between a British subject and an ordinary resident. I can well understand why a person who is not a British subject is not permitted to vote, or to be 'a municipal councillor, a member of the legislature, or a member of Parliament, and why none but British subjects should act as jurors, but I cannot see why any person who resides in Canada and has the interests of the country at heart should not be given the privilege of denouncing cases of this kind to the commission. The minister may retort that in the days prior to 1911 we had similar provisions in certain of our Acts, particularly the Act referring to combines in restraint of trade; but I would point out to him that in those days it was a comparatively easy matter for a person to become a British subject. It required three years' residence then; now in some cases I understand it requires ten years, and in many cases a person can never hope to become a British subject. Why should we put obstacles in the way of citizens of this country as is sought to be done in this Bill? I cannot see any reason for the theory which would restrict to British subjects only the denunciation of offenders to the commission. Why not extend it to every person resident in this eoutnry? Have only British subjects

knowledge necessary to denounce cases oi this kind, or is it an extra privilege given to a person who happens to be possessed of British citizenship?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As the hon. member himself intimates this restriction is in the original Combines Act, and the reason doubtless is this-and it is just as pertinent to-day as it was then, whatever its force may be. One of the avenues through which the Act may be abused is that out of malice on. envy; for .sinister reasons and not for public reasons, persons may set it in motion to secure considerable publicity and very greatly injure a rival. It was thought no doubt, and is thought still, that there should not be allowed to citizens of another country, possibly interested themselves in competing concerns across the border, an opportunity to put this Act in motion, to, as it were, hold a club over the head of a rival Canadian concern, to rack rent, to harrass, merely for their own purposes. Surely there are enough British subjects in Canada to bring to the attention of the commission any wrongdoing of this kind without having recourse to citizens of other countries. Furthermore, I do not think it will add anything to the Act to accept the amendment, for the reason that this board can move of their own motion, and if the board get information from any source, though the party informing may be given no status because not a British subject, and might not rank as an informant later, nevertheless the board might then take it up of its own motion if it saw fit to order an investigation.

I am still unconvinced. Let us take, for example, the case of an individual who is not a British subject and who wishes to denounce to the Department of Customs a case of smuggling, which might have effects as far-reaching as a denunciation under this particular Act- does the minister contend that a person who is not a British subject could not give such information to the customs officers? This Act is for the protection of the citizens of Canada, and no matter from what source the information comes, if it is useful to the country to have the information we should accept it, irrespective of whether the party is a British' subject or not. We have our courts open here for the trial of cases, and any person can have justice whether he is a British subject or not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
But you do not have rival smugglers or rival murderers; you 291 i
do have rival business men in competing concerns, and it would not do to specially subject a Canadian competitor to the harrassment of his American competitor, when there is no reciprocal right given to our own citizen.
The minister seems to think it would be a case of harrassing on the part of one concern against another.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It might be.

Very often a stranger is
in a better position to give information in regard to working conditions in Canada than the Canadian himself. Very often these concerns may be competing against each other, they may be, to use a slpck term, attempting to cut each other's throats; but there is an old saying: When thieves fall out honest men get their dues. Why not let honest men get their due when these people fall out? It seems to me that this amendment ought to be concurred in by the House.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The board can use any information they obtain that way, so the clause is all right as it is.

I am against the principle, Mr. Chairman, of making distinctions between British subjects and other residents of Canada when there is no reason for such distinction. I am not convinced that the reason given by the minister is a sound one it is not even a plausible one, and I would press my amendment.

Is it not a principle of British law that all Well-behaved citizens of our country, whether British subjects or inot, should have the same facilities open to them for the redress of wrong? Are not the courts open to the denizens of the country, as distinguished from the citizens of the country, as freely as. to the citizens themselves? I speak temperately, but I trust I speak strongly, when I say that, this is an example of an attempt to create different classes of citizens in this country, against which I protest with all my force.
I do not wish to delay the House, but I shall support the proposal of the member of George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs).
Amendment negatived: Yeas 12, nays 19.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why is it not permissible to maike application to the Chief Commissioner as well as to any one of the other commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The powers of the Chief Commissioner are supervisory in this re-

gard; be revises all orders made by any of the other commissioners. It takes two commissioners to refuse; one commissioner to grant. If the commissioner below grants, all well and good; the Chief Commissioner fixes the day and hour for the investigation; if he does not grant, the Chief Commissioner may reverse the decision.

It strikes me that when any person makes a complaint, it should be the duty of the board to investigate; the person who makes the complaint should not be obliged to prosecute. If a man has a complaint about the freight rates charged by a railway company, all he has to do is to bring the matter to the notice of the Board of Railway Commissioners. He does not have to furnish counsel or carry on the case; it is the duty of the board to take the matter up and deal with it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the hon. member is satisfied with the law as regards the Railway Commission, he must be satisfied with this legislation, because the provision in the matter to which he refers is precisely the same in both cases. The provision is in section 31 of the Board of Commerce Act, and also in section 6 of this Act. Before the Railway Commission many a man appears accompanied by counsel, as does many a company; but the board has disposition over costs and even has power to apply to the Governor in Council for the appointment of special counsel to argue on behalf of any one in any special matter. The duties of this board are expressed in just the same language as are the duties of the Board of Railway Commissioners; there is no difference.

I do not think the minister will get much from this section. When a business man thinks he is paying too much by way of freight rates, it is worth Ms while to obtain legal advice and carry on a case before the Railway Commission, but the poor consumer who pays a little more for his food than he should pay is not quite in the same position. Unless the minister expects this provision to be a dead letter he should, by some specific language, impose on this board the duty of prosecuting any case brought to their attention.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: You could not do that, because when the matter is brought to their attention they may be convinced that there is no case at all.
Assuming there is *a case.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, they must exercise their discretion as to whether, there is a case or noit, but if there is, then, the duty of dealing with the matter is imposed upon them in the most specific way.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 11-full and expeditious inquiry by board:

Paragraph 4 of this section provides that whenever in the opinion of the board an offence has been committed against this section, the board may remit to the Attorney General copies of the record of the case, with a statement of the facts, and so on. What machinery is provided for compelling the Attorney-General to act should he see fit not to take any steps in the matter?'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no machinery; I do not think this Government would have power to impose any obligation on the Attorney General of a province.
The whole matter, then, is in the hands of the Attorney General, who may deal with it as he sees fit?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes; it could not be ahy other way. The obligation stares him in the face; the facts are brought to his door; the accused is brought to his door. I think you can depend upon the Attorney General in such a case as that; he is quite likely to consider it his duty to take action.
I hope he will.

Should not the Department of Justice follow these matters up and themselves bring them to a conclusion? Is it not a weakness in the Act that the bo*ard refers such matters as this to the Attorney General of the provinces? Should it not- be the duty of the board to compel a man to carry out its orders, rather than to turn these cases over to some one else who may or may not prosecute?

That same argument, carried to its logical conclusion, would mean that the Department of Justice would take over from the Attorneys General of all the provinces the administration of our criminal law.
But this is a special board that is sitting for the prosecution of certain offences.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have no courts with paraphernalia to try, with juries and the like of that. We could, of course, take over

the work that the Attorney General of a province does and bring the facts before the courts of a province, conduct the prosecution and secure a possible conviction.
But if we should do that for this
11 p.m. offence, we ought to do it in the case of theft, of assault. We lay down a law and say that if a man commits that offence, he is offending against society; he is guilty of a crime against the Code. Then it becomes the duty of the Crown authorities of the province to prosecute for an offence that is actually committed. Here we go further than we go in any other case; we collect die facts; we pick out the offender, and we bring the facts and the offender to the door of the Attorney General. If we go further than that, we might as well go the whole road.
I (Mr. JACOBS':	In cases of offences
against the Bank Act, offences by bank managers, presidents and so on, it has been customary for the Dominion authorities to take the matter up. I have in mind the case of the Ville Marie bank, in which case the Solicitor General came from Ottawa to Montreal and prosecuted, on behalf of the department men who were implicated in the wrecking of the bank.
, Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR: It is not an extraordinary thing for the Dominion Government to prosecute offenders against Acts of this kind. It is the most common thing; it is done in the Customs Department, and at present the Inland Revenue Department has detectives going through Nova Scotia and bringing prosecutions against people who violate the law regarding putting stamps on the goods they sell. The prosecution is conducted, not by the Attorney General of the province, but under the direction of the (Minister of Inland Revenue. The Fisheries Act is another ease. It is a very common thing to find a man who violates the fishery regulations prosecuted under the direction of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. If the minister does not provide some machinery by which the Department of Justice or some other department will carry out the provisions of the Act, in seeing that the offenders are punished, the Act will he a dead letter.

I can confirm the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs) as regards the Ville Marie Bank case, in which I remember that the Department of Justice was represented by the then Solicitor General, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Only represented. He did not conduct the case.
Yes, he did. I was for the defence in that case with Senator Foster and Mr. Greenshields, K.C.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Who represented the
province?
The Crown Prosecutor was there, but the case was in the hands of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, then Solicitor General.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the prosecutor had entered a nolle prosequi, where would Sir Charles Fitzpatrick have been?
I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He would have had to go home.

The minister is supposing an impossible case. Here was a clear case of fraud, and it created quite a stir at the time. Hundreds of people were ruined, and the Government took action immediately. I remember Sir Charles Fitzpatrick remaining in court for days and weeks conducting the case personally. I addressed the jury for the defence, and he addressed the jury for the Crown. I remember other cases where the department was directly represented by a gentleman who became later treasurer of the province of Quebec, the Hon. Mr. Hall. He represented the Post Office Department in cases where men had been arrested because they had 'tampered with His Majesty's mails.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

There the Department of Justice was directly represented. I remember one case, because the man who was implicated in that robbery was well known and had very strong influence. The people were surprised when they learned the name of the accused. I was Crown Prosecutor myself.
Is there anything in this measure to prevent the Federal Government from being represented ? My hon. friend says that it remains within the jurisdiction of the province.

We claim that the department should take direct action in the matter. I was Crown prosecutor for several years in Montreal, and on many occasions the Federal Government was represented on criminal cases.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What kind of cases?
Cases in which Federal Acts had been violated.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Where the revenue of the Dominion of Canada or where a public service of the Dominion is concerned, we frequently are represented, and we could be represented here if we chose..
Why do not you choose?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But in no case, except in such as that, is the Government represented, let alone does it conduct the prosecution and. take over the administration of justice from the province. Will the hon. member tell me why it would be the duty of the Government, for a violation of the Combines and Fair Prices Act, to take over the duties of the Crown Prosecutor, conduct the case before the court, and why it would not be the duty in any other case of violation of the Criminal Code? If the case is as the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) mentions where we are collecting our own revenue, the province is not particularly interested in that, and we have to look after the case?
What about the fishery laws, where you are not collecting any revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not had that brought to my attention, but I will guarantee that, if they are merely offences that are created by statute, we do not take over the prosecution. The tendency of the people of this country is altogether too much towards looking to the Federal Government to overlap and duplicate all the provincial machinery. Under the pressure of careless criticism, careless newspaper . publicity, people are getting the idea that Provincial Governments and municipal governments under them are nothing more nor less than forms, and if there is anything really to be done, the only institution to do it is the Federal Government of Canada, and some of them,-the unreasoning ones, whose opinions I fear are fed by statements such as some we have heard to-night, not the great public of this country-want us to have a police force in every county and every town, and if any Federal law is violated, they want us immediately to come in and enforce that Federal law, as if we had not all the machinery of the provinces that is at present used in enforcing Federal laws of a criminal or semi-criminal character. Think what it would cost the people of this country if the Dominion is asked to duplicate the whole machinery for the enforcement of law, for the prosecution of offenders that now exists, and has long been established in every province of

the Dominion. We talk about having too much Government; this would be simply pyramiding it.
They have it in the United States. [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, they do not have it in the States, and even if they had it in a thousand States, I do not want to see follies that other people commit, committed here.
I do not consider them follies.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not doubt that. That would be a good thing for the lawyers. It would mean a duplication of Crown prosecutors. There can be no greater folly than the invasion of provincial jurisdiction, the duplication of provincial machinery, the multiplication of office holders, the pyramiding of Government such as is suggested to-night.
The machinery there exists. We do everything in our power, more than we can be called upon constitutionally to do. We create the offence; that is our duty. We have an organization that collects the facts and points out the offender. We draw this to the attention of the attorney general whose duty it is under the constitution to prosecute. Surely it is the duty of this Parliament to refrain from interfering with the acknowledged ambit of provincial authority.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman's Latin should be permitted with impunity to confuse the House.
That is an insinuation against the House. They understand it very well.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Seven-eighths of the Criminal Code is malum prohibitum, precisely as this is. The hon. gentleman says you cannot expect the Attorney 'General of a province to act in the case of an offence against this law, but you could expect him to act in the case of an offence against the Code. You could not expect public opinion, he says, to force the Attorney General to act in the administration of justice and the punishment of offences in respect of which it is his duty to act, but you could expect him to act in another case under the Code. Let us see. We will assume that somebody interferes with the logging booms of a big lumber corporation-perhaps moves them by night. He says that you could depend on the Attorney General to act in a case of that sort because public opinion would be so aroused -being malum in se, that the Attorney General would be forced to act. But if some profiteer is, in the words of hon. gentlemen opposite, starving the children of the poor while the husband prays for relief, you cannot expect the Attorney General to be moved at all because that is merely malum prohibitum, and you could not expect public opinion to take any interest in it. The only case in which public opinion would take an interest, he says, is where somebody interferes with the rights of private individuals. If somebody by his conduct oppresses the poor and goes rampant through the country as a profiteer, public opinion is not going to take any interest, and consequently the Attorney 'General will not act. That is his argument. There is no argument in the world that can relieve the Attorney General from the prosecutiQn of offences created by this Act that will not relieve him also from the prosecution of offences created by the Code. Furthermore, we have ample power to appear and be represented if we choose. But is it wisdom on the part of the Parliament of Canada expressly to relieve the province of the duty cast upon it by Confederation, and especially to take i't from them and make it ours without any consent on their part? I will never be a party to relieving them from that obligation, I do not think it would be in the interest of the country as a whole. It would be most expensive in the way of duplication of machinery and duplication of costs, and no reason in the world exists for it. We can be represented, the Act is strong enough to enable us 'to be so, but we surely should decline to bring on the head of the Parliament and Government of Canada obligations that are fixed by the constitution as primarily belonging to the provinces.

You do not need 'to put the Attorney General in at all. If you really desire to accomplish good by this legislation, and intend to investigate offences and follow them up to a prosecution, there is no necessity to say in this Act that the matter will be handed over to the Attorney General. We are setting up an expensive court; we are providing large salaries for the commissioners; we are instituting a new department of government, and naturally we want it to do some good, if the minister will not take any interest in the matter, the Act goes for nothing; it is not worth the paper it is written on if the department will not follow up the offences and see that the offenders are punished.

The commission is going to conduct an investigation. It will examine witnesses, gather information and then pitchfork the whole thing over to the Attorney General. In my province the municipalities pay for the criminal prosecutions brought by the Attorney General. What municipality is going to be responsible for this? We have no system by which the Government of my province take up criminal cases and pay for them. They may engage a solicitor to represent the Attorney General at a certain * court, but the expenses of the court are paid by the municipalities. This is not a new proposal, Two or three sessions ago we had a question relating to the transportation of intoxicating liquors, and the Minister of Justice proposed a measure prohibiting the export of liquor into a dry area. It was drawn to his attention that the statute would be ineffective if it was not prosecuted by the Federal Government, and the Minister of Justice inserted a clause making it the duty of the Justice Department to conduct those prosecutions. The department has agents in the several cities where these offences are committed, and they are well equipped for conducting these prosecutions where they should be conducted. If the minister refuses to provide in this Act that the prosecution shall be followed up by the Department of Justice and the offenders punished, we may as well discard the Act, because it will not he worth anything for the purpose for which it is intended.

Suppose the duty is imposed upon the Attorney General of, say, Nova Scotia. He has no funds to pay for the prosecution. Nothing has been voted by the legislature for that purpose. We want something done this year, and how is it expected that anything will be done promptly if a duty is imposed upon an officer who has no funds and cannot have any before the legislature meets again?
iMr. MORPHY: The hon. gentleman says that in Nova Scotia there are no funds.
No funds appropriated.
No funds available.
I said appropriated.

I will use my own word. In one province in Canada, for the administration of public justice, provision 'h'as not been made* either by the province itself or by the Federal Government, for the prosecution of offenders under a criminal or quasi-criminal act.
No criminals there.

If that is the state of affairs it is about time it should be remedied. I really do not feel that the hon. member for Antigonish and Guys-borough is entirely honest-without any malice in the term-in attempting to make us believe that an Act of Parliament, designed to cure an evil which it is eminently in the public interest to abolish, will not be enforced by those charged) with the administration of justice in Nova Scotia. The hon. member and others, h'ave spoken of the heinous sin of permitting to run rampant throughout the country combine men and profiteers and those engaged in the unholy and ungodly mergers, trust and combines. Surely the public sentiment in Nova Scotia would be such that if the Government of that province could not supply funds to prosecute cases under this Act the necessary money would come out of private pockets. In my opinion, nothing in Canada would sooner elicit funds from any government to prosecute a clear case or one that is open to grave suspicion, than any case

of unholy profiteering or a combination to enhance the prices of food to the poor man, in whom hon. gentlemen on both sides are interested. Will the hon. gentleman tell me that if any Federal Act of a quasi-criminal nature, applicable throughout Canada, is infringed in Nova Scotia, the Attorney General of that Province in the past has not been in the habit of setting the law in motion whether the Dominion asked him to or not?
The Attorney General of Nova Scotia can say to the Dominion Government: You should enforce your own Act.
It is a sham.
My question is: Does the hon. member know of a case in which the Attorney General or the Government of Nova 'Scotia asked this Government to enforce its own Act because it was a Federal Act?
The proposal was never made.

So my hon. friend (Mr. J. H. Sinclair) is proceeding upon the assumption that something will happen that never has happened. I repeat again that the argument of the hon. gentleman shows an utter lack of faith in the public administration of justice by the provincial officers of the Government of Nova Scotia. I think it is unworthy of a public man in this House, unless he has ground for such an accusation, to throw a stigma upon the Attorney General of Nova Scotia and the officers charged with the administration of justice in that province, by saying that in a great public abuse of this kind those officials would refuse to prosecute where it
was their plain and whole duty. I do not think there is anything in the argument; it is just a little bit of diversion because it is half-past eleven in the evening.

I repudiate the statement that I endeavoured to throw any stigma upon the Attorney General of Nova Scotia and the prosecuting officials in that province, and I throw the imputation back upon my hon. friend who is supporting a Government which is professing to put down combines and will not spend a dollar of money in prosecuting its own law.

Might I point this out to the committee: these prosecutions may take place in a remote part of the Dominion, j do not want to say in Nova Scotia, but as I do not see any member from Prince Edward Island in the House, I will take that province for the purpose of my illustration.
The hon. member for King's (Mr. Mclsaac) is in his seat.

I had hoped he was asleep.
tvtt- BUREAU i No, lie never sleeps.

Well, let us take the case, for instance, of a large sugar refinery located in Summerside or Charlottetown, and which does business throughout the entire Dominion. Perhaps most of its business is done in British Columbia, or at any rate in the West, but it is located in Prince Edward Island for the reason that it is. near tide-water and there happens to be plenty of water-power in the district. Why should the province of Prince Edward Island be obliged to prosecute these cases simply because the head office of that institution is situated in that province? If the minister is not prepared to adopt our suggestion that the proceedings should be instituted by the Attorney General or the Minister of Justice of Canada, we would suggest as an alternative that at least an official from the Department of Justice attend in every case, because if that be not done this law need not be passed-it is going to be an absolute dead letter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
suggest that there should be a clause in this Act making it the duty of the Attorney General for the Dominion to prosecute offenders against this law in provincial courts?
Yes, that is to say that the private prosecutor should 'be the Justice Department.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I see what my hon.
friend's mind is up to now. Here is an indictable offence created, and the hon. gentleman knows that nobody can prosecute except the provincial authorities.
Mr. JAiCOBiS: I want to know where it is stated in the Bill that this is an indictable offence?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Everywhere in the Bill, in every word and sentence. There must be an indictment laid, and the hon. member knows as well as I do that no one can lay the indictment but the Attorney General-it cannot be done.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Because nobody has
power to lay an indictment; it must come through the Crown, represented by the province. We may toe represented, we may be there when the case comes up, we may even take part, but the whole thing is under the supervision and absolute authority of the Attorney General.
That is because it is made so by this Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, because it is an indictable offence. You cannot make it an indictable offence and have a prosecution in any other way. The hon. member, if he has ever practised in the criminal courts, knows that.
It is because I have practised in the criminal courts that I do not admit it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will not say that any one except the Crown, in the right of the province, can lay an indictment in the courts of the province.
No, a criminal indictment is laid by the Attorney General.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly,
But there is always a private prosecutor.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, tout he must secure the Crown's approval and the Crown must lay the indictment.
In theory, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, in practice, in
everything. He may start it just as we start this, but he cannot go. any further; it must be the duty altogether of the Cbown to prosecute. I tell the hon. gentleman the private prosecutor cannot constitutionally do it, and I know he knows that. Why, 
if we were represented there we must take the indictment as laid by the Crown. We may be anxious to go on, but if the province quits we have to quit too. Is that the way the hon. gentleman wants to face the prosecution for these offences? So that somebody else should be there to represent this Government and be under the care of the provincial authorities? That is absurd. The cases to which the hon. member (Mr. J. <H. Sinclair) refers to are prosecutions for offences against fishery regulations before the magistrates. Anybody can appear there; the Crown does not need to take charge of those cases at all, of any prosecution for offences against fishery regulations or for collection of inland revenue. These are not indictable offences, they are mere prosecutions before magistrates. But when you make an offence an. indictable one it becomes part of the Criminal Code of Canada, and the conduct of the prosecution must absolutely-I repeat the phrase; there is no escape from it-be under the . charge wholly of the Attorney General of the province.

Although we are creating
entirely new legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Certainly. Every time
you create an indictable offence you are creating new legislation; the hon. gentleman knows that.

In conclusion, I may say
to the minister that if he proposes that the Attorney General shall take charge of these cases without any assistance from the Justice Department, we may just as well throw this Bill into the waste paper basket.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the Attorney General of the provinces intend to recede from their constitutional obligations which nobody else can perform no matter how willing or anxious they may be, then we cannot enforce the law in this country; there is no other way of doing it. It is either this way or no other way. But I do not have that feeling towards the Attorneys General of the provinces of Canada, nor do the people. I believe public opinion will force any recalcitrant 'Attorney General to prosecute these cases; I do not think there is any doubt about it. If it does not then the case cannot be prosecuted, because there is no other way in which it can be done.
Unless assistance is given to the Attorney General how is relief going to be given to the people?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows we are going to give it just by the way we axe doing it here. It cannot be done in any other way unless the constitution is changed, and we cannot change it.
(Mr. BUREAU: The offence in question is not created here by the law but is created by the Board.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The offence? No.

You charge me with being in a combine or merger, or doing something contrary to the provisions of this law. An investigation is held and the result is an order by the Board declaring that my conduct complained of is illegal? Is not that the process?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

And that I ought not to do it. Now the remedy is in the Board. They say: " You have got to desist from doing such a thing within a scheduled time." An order is made by the board which is absolute and fines are provided, not because I am acting in a combine but because I refuse to acknowledge the order of the board.
And the money goes into the Dominion treasury.

I want to be clear about that. I am not fined because I have been guilty of forming part of a combine, or doing something which is enumerated in this Act as being illegal; the fine is imposed because I refuse to desist from doing a thing, or refuse to do .something which I am ordered by the Board to do. Is not that the gist of the whole legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is the offence.
The offence is the result of my refusing to obey the Board.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Very good.
It is not an absolute offence, it is a contingent offence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It becomes absolute.

The offence under the Act is not that I form part of a combine, but the offence is in my refusing to obey the order of the board, which is established for the purpose of preventing combines, or of dissolving them if they exist. If I comply with the order when issued there is no offence. The offence is found by the board, not by the law. My hon. friend smiles, but there is a distinction to be made. If the statute said: Whosoever shall be found guilty of doing or not doing a certain thing shall be liable to a fine-there would be an
offence. But you say that this board shall have power to make orders, and if any particular order is obeyed there is no offence. It is just the enforcement practically of what I would call a civil judgment. You are to do this; if you do not do it you are liable to pay a fine; and if you do not pay a fine you are liable to go to jail. The section says that the board is to hold an investigation, the evidence is to be taken down and then sent to the Attorney General. The Attorney General has not got to decide whether or not there is an offence and then prosecute the man; but he has to bring him forward and say: Here is an order of the board for you to do this; you did not do it; you are liable to a fine. How is he going to collect it? The grand jury have found that indictment; that grand jury is the board. Then he wants the man to be prosecuted before the petit jury on the indictment found by the board
the grand jury. I do not see how it could be done in that way. If you say: You are in a combine; you are, liable to such and such a penalty-then you bring the case to the grand jury and submit your evidence, and if they find a true bill you have me found guilty of being one of a combine. That follows the ordinary course. But here is the collection of a fine. I do not see why execution should not be issued on the return made by you to the Superior Court in oui province, say, the sheriff would then go down to seize the property, and if there was nothing to seize the man would be put in jail. Take a case of slander in our courts. If the man cannot pay the money which he is condemned to pay we have a certain procedure under our civil courts; he appears before a judge and the judge sentences him to go to jail. This is the same process. It is a civil process, and I do not see how you can bring it before the criminal courts the way the Bill is drafted. What offence are you going to find before the grand jury?-of not obeying an order of the board.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Exactly.
That is not an offence.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We make it so.

You may; but look at the position you are putting that grand jury in. They have sat there and said: You did not obey the court. That is a true bill. You go before the petit jury, and the fact is admitted that he refused to obey. You take that judgment to the superior court, and the sheriff goes and tries to collect the fine, and if he cannot collect it, then the man is liable to imprisonment. That is a purely civil proceeding. I have never practised

before criminal courts, but I have practised enough before the civil courts to know that this is just the same as an action for slander.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The man may not be fined at all. For the life of me I do not see the point my hon. friend is trying to make. This creates an indictable offence, or it does not.
It ought not to.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is another thing. It the hon. gentleman does not want to make an offence against an order of the board an indictable offence, all right; make it simply an offence.
Punishable by imprisonment. You do not have to bring him before the jury.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: How far can you go in that way?
You can go any length at all under our procedure. When a man is subject to a fine or imprisonment, and. he does not pay the fine, .you take him to jail.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Certainly. We provide here that you need not go before the jury, but we make the offence of that character that it is indictable. It is one thing whether we chose to do that or not, but if this Bill passes it does that. That being so, it does not matter what we declare constitutes the offence. We might declare, if we chose to do so that a man who goes in a flying machine commits an indictable offence; instead of that we say that a man who disobeys an order of the board commits an indictable offence. Once we have said that, then this is the only way in which proceedings looking to punishment can be [DOT] carried on. If the hon. gentleman wants to move-
I do not want to move anything. I am suggesting a cheaper way of reaching the same end.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We cannot proceed in any other way than this.

It is a cheaper way and an easier way of letting the law follow its course and getting a man to jail, instead of having to come and say: On such a day he disobeyed an order contrary to Bill 167, as in such case made and provided for. Then you have got to go before the grand jury and the petit jury, and to do that you have to wait until the assizes are convened. We have some districts in

our province where they do not have criminal assizes more than once in two years. If you follow the ordinary civil procedure, the moment a return is made by the sheriff or the bailiff that there are no goods upon which he can execute judgment, you just make up your return, and that return is prima facie evidence to make application to have the man jailed. What you want is the punishment, not the procedure. This is the easiest and, it seems to me, the most logical procedure to follow. Of course, I do not know how it would work in the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If you do not make the offence an indictable one you put it in the hands of magistrates to completely circumvent you.
No, it does not go before a magistrate. It is an executory judgment. There is no appeal about it. If the man has not sufficient property to pay the fine he goes to jail.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would necessitate giving the man the option of a fine in every case. That is the first objection. But the next objection is fatal, that that law does not apply to the rest of Canada at all.
Have you not got that procedure in slander?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

As the matter is very urgent and serious, I want to discuss the irrigation feature of the Estimate and to endeavour to impress upon the House the fact that the matter is not wholly a local question, but one of a good deal of national importance as well. Hon. -members have all heard in the past of the situation in the southern part of AlbeTta, and I might also be permitted to include the southern part of Saskatchewan, both of which pass through dry years and consequently have crop failures; and although they have good years with abnormal crops, still every few years they suffer adversity. I am afraid that this year the situation has become so serious that it is necessary for action to be taken in order to retain in that country the people who have been there for some years and who have been fighting the adverse conditions We have in southern Alberta several irrigation systems; one of them, which is in my county has been a great success, and dry years do not have any effect on the success of irrigated farming. What I would argue here to-night is an extension of irrigation in order to safeguard the people who are in that part of the country and also to protect Canada as a nation from loss, and certainly loss would be suffered if those people were forced to leave Canada at this time. We brought them into this country; we practically told them that the land they were taking up was suitable for agriculture. If we made a mistake, we must admit it now. But they were brought in under our auspices; they have spent their capital and endeavoured to make a success of agriculture theire.	I do not say that they have
not made a success when weather conditions have been good and they have been able to enjoy a proper amount of moisture. There is no question about the fer-

tility of the soil because under fair conditions they have very good crops, and in the years 1915 and 1916 I am satisfied that in that area the average yield per acre will compare with that of any country in the world. This year there is no question that a great part of southern Alberta will be subject to crop failure again.
12 m. What have we to do to retain those people in the country? My answer to the question is that we should endeavour to extend that irrigation system m order to provide them with the moisture that will enable the soil to produce crops that will add to the wealth of the country. I maintain that irrigation produces wealth, produces it every year. Mr. C. A. Magrath, Chairman of the International Waterways Commission, who was probably the first man to interest himself in irrigation in Western Canada, returned only a few days ago from a trip to southern Alberta and I understand he stated that, in the irrigated country adjacent to Lethbridge, there would be a million dollars worth of alfalfa produced this year, and that is only one section of this particular system. I was talking also to the Deputy Minister of Agriculture to-day, and he told me that his information from the experimental farm at Lethbridge was to the effect that the drv portion of that farm would produce prac tically nothing this year, but that on the irrigated portion conditions were exceptionally good. That proved that irrigation used with the soil of southern Alberta will produce great crops no matter how adverse the conditions may generally be.
It might be argued that it was a mistake to settle portions of this country be' cause of the frequent droughts, and the loss of crops. But, on the other hand, the people are there, and we should try to keep them in this country if at all possible. If they leave this country, that will certainly be a black eye to Western Canada, because the views they express of conditions in one section of the country will be made to apply to the whole couritry and will probably not do justice to that. My argument is that we should use all the available water supply and bring it to the land in southern Alberta so as to enable these people to remain there and to safeguard the amount of money we have already spent to bring those people into the country and to keeep them there. Those of us who were in the last Parliament know that, in 1914, we had to provide a great deal of money for relief, not only for 
stock, but for the people themseslves in order to carry them through the fall, winter and spring. It is almost certain that some relief will have to be provided this year, I do not say by this Government, because under present conditions the lands have been patented and assistance of that kind comes largely from the provincial government. But the irrigation problem which I am trying to present to the House to-night is a matter which I want this Government and this Parliament to consider seriously in order to meet this situation. I have before me letter from one of the principal organizations in the city of Lethbridge, and it states the matter so concisely that I think I shall read it in order that the committee may have the opinion of an organization of business men in southern Alberta. The letter reads:
The majority of thinking men in this district have long been of the opinion that ultimately irrigation must come if the south is to go forward, and seeing the main feature is not lacking, viz., an ample water supply, we feel that effort should be made to avoid any unnecessary delay.
As you are aware, the territory from Pincher Creek on the west and Swift Current on the east,-a distance of approximately three hundred miles,-and from the International boundary on the south to the Red Deer River on the north,-a distance of about two hundred miles, -requires irrigation and we are of the opinion that this area could be largely irrigated.
As you will remember, 1910, 1914, 1917 and 191S, have been practically complete crop failures, and we regret to advise you that the *crop prospects this year, on account of drought, are likely to be a repetition of the years above mentioned. We are now convinced that irrigation is of vital importance if we are to retain the farmers in this territory. It will not only be a local benefit but of national importance on. account of the enormously increased production. The unanimous opinion of tne Rotary Club was in favour of having the Dominion Government appoint a commission of say three able men in whom both the Government and the public would have confidence, to oome West immediately and investigate the whole question of irrigation, and suggest ways and means of getting this put into operation, also to look into conditions as they prevail at the present time. There is no doubt but that a large number of fanners will have to receive aid from the Government as in 1914.
That is the prevalent view of the people who are living in that section of the country. In presenting this case to the committee and the Government, and in advocating the expansion of irrigation, I do not want the impression to be conveyed that this means an outlay of money on the part of the Dominion or of any Government in the country that would be invested and not returned in any way, because under the irrigation systems as they have prevailed in

Western Canada the people who use irrigation practically pay for the systems which are brought into existence. But it has rested with this Government and must rest with it in the future to carry on the surveys in order that the people may learn what lands are suitable for irrigation. Once they find out what land's can be irrigated it is possible for irrigation districts to be formed, and these districts should be in the position to bring the water into the district to be distributed over the land requiring irrigation. In raising the actual money there may be difficulty, but with assistance from the Government by way of guarantees it would' be possible to get the money to enable irrigation to be provided for these districts, and then the problem would be solved.
I want to emphasize, before I sit down, the fact that the situation is extremely serious, that we are in danger of losing, I would say, probably a thousand or more farmers in that section of the country if we do not come to their rescue by adopting a policy that will enable them to obtain irrigation without delay. If we can obtain irrigation without delay I am quite certain we can retain these people in the country, and with irrigation they will be able to produce a great deal more than they have ever been able to produce in the most auspicious years in the past, because we know that in that particular country wherever irrigation is practised the yield is doubled and even trebled in some cases.
Another matter I would point out is this, that under irrigation hay crops of all kinds can be raised, and these hay crops provide the means of encouraging mixed farming and enabling farmers to go into stock raising. The more of it we have, the better it will be for mixed farming in that part of the country that is to be irrigated. I would urge upon the minister that some action should be taken without delay to inquire into the extension of irrigation to meet the urgent need at this time. I want to say also that while it is a matter affecting my constituency, I feel it is of greater importance than a local question. It reaches out into a national question, because if these people were to leave our country and carry across the line or to any other country stories of failure in agriculture in Western Canada, it would do a great deal of damage to the whole country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think I should put on record a few words on this question. The
merits of the policy of irrigation, if from a business standpoint and an engineering standpoint practicable, cannot of course be disputed and the special need of irrigation in the territory ,to which my hon. friend refers is so pronounced that he only does his duty in impressing it forcibly on hon. members. There are in many parts of southern Alberta large areas of territory of the utmost fertility, but the curse of which is repeated drought. The experience of the last few years has been that that drought is so frequently repeated that the ultimate value of the land may be very problematical indeed unless irrigation is proven to be feasible. If proven to be feasible, then the value of that portion of Canada becomes enhanced accordingly. Every portion of this Dominion is interested in its development and success. It is quite true, as the hon. gentleman says, that discouragement has followed discouragement and that thousands of settlers who have come into the country under the encouragement of federal and provincial authorities may be compelled to leave. Consequently it is the duty of Parliament and the duty of the Government to take the most generous position that we constitutionally can take arid justify, with regard to irrigation development. Some correspondence has been carried on and several conferences have been held between myself and the provincial governments in regard to this matter. I have taken the position that the general problem of irrigation, in so far as actual development is concerned, is a provincial obligation. On the contrary, the province has assumed a rather different position. Hitherto the Dominion has undertaken survey and engineering work with a view to deciding as to the engineering feasibility of the project, and I had no objection to continuing that responsibility and the expenditure that is entailed thereby; but I felt, for the reason particularly that there was no Dominion land that was to be benefited by irrigation development, the whole being privately-owned land, that the time had come when we should have an understanding that the obligation of the Dominion with regard to irrigation ceased at the point of the completion of the survey and engineering work. I felt that if we continued longer without that understanding, the province and the people of the province would more and more get the impression that the whole problem of irrigation was federal and not provincial, and would look with increasing confidence and indeed with increased imperativeness to the Dominion authorities to continue obliga-

tions with regard to irrigation right into the development sphere itself.
Consequently, after prolonged correspondence and after many conferences where we failed to agree, we finally came to an understanding, and the Provincial Government acquiesced in our position that we should not be called upon to undertake further responsibility after we had undertaken and discharged the work of surveying the whole field and of engaging the engineering forces necessary for that purpose. We propose, now that we have come to an understanding, to carry it out on our part to the full and to interpret that understanding generously. Already I have instructed that to be done, and as a consequence the item that appears in the estimate now before the House, $60,000, has been placed there for surveying and engineering work, under the Irrigation Act, in the North Lethbridge district. This Parliament must give increasing attention to the responsibilities that we have entered into in this regard, and must take increasing interest in the subject so ably brought to our attention by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan). What is this gas well at Pelican Rapids?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It was bored by the Geological Department as it was then, in 1897. Gas was struck at a certain depth and it burst forth and destroyed the well, which has roared ever since so loudly that at times, years ago, you could hear it ten miles away. There was a fire there for many years but it is now extinguished. I had been seeking for parties competent to close this well.
I have heard of arrangements that could be made, and have followed them up only to meet with discouragement and failure. But at last I have made an arrangement that I think is satisfactory with a competent company who have undertaken to close this well. I think the maximum that can be charged is $15,000-that is the utmost they can take-but I have arranged a sliding scale whereby if the work is done in a certain way it will be rather cheap. If the company can succeed in that way it will be in their own interest as well as ours, and will cost very much less.

Department of Trade and Commerce. To provide for Civil Government, additional amount required, $18,700.

speechtext: I see in the Main Estimates that 83 new employees are asked for, and in the Supplementary Estimates there is something over 100. Public Works-slides and 'booms, graving docks, locks and flams, etc., working expenses, etc., $ 170,fj00.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I feel that I ought to
make an explanation of this vote, because I am attempting to make some radical changes in the operation of these works. A system has grown up, dating, I think, from pre-Confederation days, under which the Government has spent a very large amount of money in providing slides, booms and things of that kind for the benefit of the lumbermen on various rivers-the Gatineau, the St. Maurice, the Saguenay, and some of the upper branches of the Ottawa
292i
river. It would surprise the Committee if they could realize how much money has been expended on these works. For many years, under the method of bookkeeping which prevailed, a profit was shown, but that method did not take into consideration the overhead expenses at head office, which are very large. In fact, the thing is a dumping ground for people for whom no other place can be found and who are put on these slides and booms.
For their health?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: No, for their daily bread. Of late years we have been going behind pretty rapidly. Before I came into the department an arrangement was made under which ,the slides and booms on the St. Maurice river were handed over to a local company who pay a certain rental for them, and 'the principle is so good that I have endeavoured to follow it out. On the Gatineau we have not been going behind as much as we have at the other places, but we have been losing around $1,000 a year for the last five or six years, although from the beginning a profit is shown. I have just completed an arrangement with the lumber company that are operating on the Gatineau river; I am practically giving them the whole thing to get rid of it and save a loss. My reason for doing that is that we are up against the expenditure of a very large amount, probably $35,000 or $40,000, or even more, in order to make these works workable, and I think it is just as well that the big lumbermen, who have not been losing any money during the last three or four years, should pay that $40,000. Anyway, we shall get rid of the obligation of maintaining a lot of very estimable gentlemen who have not been working very hard for some years. Conditions on the Ottawa river are very much worse. Last year we expended on slides and booms on the Ottawa river in the vicinity of this city, $40,106, and we got a revenue of $11,000. The year before we spent $40,000 and got a revenue of $23,000; the year before that we spent $36,000 and got a revenue of $28,000.
Without taking overhead expenses into account?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
This does not include overhead; it is simply a little bonus that we have been handing out to these poor lumbermen around Ottawa who need the money. However, I am making an effort to get rid of that end of it, too. In quite recent years they started the same beneficent system down on the Saguenay

river, and this year I refused to open the booms. I told the Price Company and other large institutions that the booms were there and that they could use them, but that we did not propose to spend any money on them-and I believe they tare getting the lumber down the river without any difficulty. The same thing happened in the Madawaska. The man who had been boom-master died and I refused to appoint another man in his place.

That is in your own coun-. ty?
Mr. iCARVELL: Oh, no, that is in Ontario. We pay our own bills down in New Brunswick; we would think that manna was coming down from the heavens if the Government provided booms and slides for our lumbermen. However, the sum and substance of it all is that in the course of another year we shall be entirely rid of this business and the lumbermen will probably get a lot of works and material that cost a great deal of money and which will be valuable to them, but which are a liability to the Government.
Could the minister not get them to pay something for these works?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I should make some explanation of this item also; these works are not a money-maker either. In the early days it was absolutely necessary, I believe, that the Government should establish telephone lines in the outlying portions of Canada, and there are many places in Canada where it is still necessary that these lines should be maintained. For instance, the line to the Yukon must be maintained. There is a line down the north shore of the 'St. Lawrence river, extending away out along the Labrador coast, which must be haaintained, and it may be that lines should be maintained down on the Gaspe coast. There are estimable people who believe that it is necessary to maintain telegraph and telephone lines in Cape Breton Island; but I have some difficulty in bringing myself to the conclusion that that is necessary. It might interest the committee if I show them the practical working out of these systems. I appointed a gentleman in whom I had absolute confidence and who made a very exhaustive study of and report upon

the whole telegraph and telephone system of Canada, and the committee will see by this item we are asking for $780,500 for the purpose of maintaining these telegraph and telephone lines.
Over and above any revenue?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am coming to that. It is hardly as bad as that," although it is pretty bad. The total expenditure is $780,500 only for maintenance and operation, not including anything for extensions. I have had a statement. prepared showing the cost of all these different lines, the cost of maintenance, the cost of operation, the revenues and the deficits, and also a report as to what, in Mr. Robinson's view, ought to be done as a business proposition.
Who is Mr. Robinson?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
He is the general manager of the New Brunswick Telephone company at (St. John, N.B. He is a man who has had a very lengthy experience in the telephone business, and without any question he is one of the Canadian experts at least on telephone business. He started work last September, and he has been working on this inquiry part of the time ever since. He went throughout the whole country, as far as Prince Rupert, Vancouver and Victoria. Without wearying the committee with details, I want to give just a little idea of the operations of these lines. The cost of running the northwestern lines in Saskatchewan last year was, in round figures, $59,000, and our revenue $8,000, or a loss of about $50,000. There are probably not more than fifteen or twenty miles in Saskatchewan that do not now have telephone or telegraphic communication by some other system. In Alberta, the cost was $78,000, and the revenue about $18,000, or a loss of about $59,000. The same remarks cannot be made with regard to Alberta, because some lines, but not very many, must be maintained. The construction of the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway through the Peace River and Grand Prairie districts has made it unnecessary that the Government should operate some of these lines, and we can get rid of a large number of them. In British Columbia, the mainland, the cost was $78,000, and the revenue $30,000, or a loss of about $48,000. In Vancouver Island the cost was $99,000, the revenue $37,000, or

a loss of albout $62,000. You have the biggest kisses on the Yukon, and that service must ibe maintained. The loss there is $133,000. Taking the whole matter, while we are asking for $780,500, to maintain these services, the revenue last year was $205,558, or a loss of about half a million dollars or over.
Mr. McMAS'TER: Without any provision for sinking fund or deterioration?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

speechtext: Does the Government contemplate the construction of any other telephone lines?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: No, excepting that in the Supplementary Estimates there are a few items for very short extensions, something that would be necessary if we go on; and if we do not, of course it would be necessary that somebody else should construct them. But they go into territory which should receive telephone communication.

What are the reasons which determine the action of the Government in granting a telephone system to a locality?
I know of a number of rural localities in Quebec, for instance, where there are county telephone systems, absolutely under our own rule. The farmers pay for the system.
I might mention the counties of Lotbiniere, Megantic, Bellechasse, part of the county of Beauce, and of the county of Dorchester.
