speechtext: My hon. friend has not kept in touch with the matter exactly, because a very modest start was made in the county of Dorchester two years ago.
I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I got rid of that. I made a trade and some local company took it off our hands. We were lucky; wo got out of that for some four or five thousand dollars. We nipped that in the bud.
As to the policy in British Columbia, it was necessary in the early days that some provision should be made for reaching the outlying districts of that province. First of all there was a telegraph system, which later on was converted into a telephone system. It was a real necessity. It is a question of policy whether the Government will hand over the telephone to some corporation or provincial or municipal body. There was a rapid telephone development in the province of Quebec in recent years. In Quebec county we have not been as successful as in Dorchester county, but we have stopped expenditures to a very large extent, and we are very much in hopes that the wires that are still on the poles will be leased to some local company; we shall have to do something or other with the system. It is not a money maker, I can assure my h(^n. friend.

There have been no telephone subsidies for the province of Quebec with the two exceptions the minister has mentioned. In Dorchester county during

the last election Mr. Sevigny, then Minister of Inland Revenue, obtained a certain grant for the building of a telephone line, and Mr. Pelletier, the late Postmaster (General, also obtained a grant for the county of Quebec. I think it is commendable that communication should be given to the outlying districts in newly settled parts of the *country, but I do not think this policy should be embarked upon by the Government to any great extent. I think we should stop granting such subsidies in the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
My hon. friend and I
will not quarrel very much about that.

There are two or three outstanding accounts in connection with the lines in Dorchester and Quebec counties which I think should be paid.
. Mr. CARVELiL:	Perhaps I should refer
*to that matter. A gentleman by the name of Martineau built telephone lines in Quebec county. The custom seems to have been to build lines, and later the money would be voted and the account paid. speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
There is certainly .a good deal of merit in that contention.
Supplementary Estimates 1919-20'-Harbours and rivers-Esquimau, B. O., new dry dock $500,000.

I want to make one statement that will cover a number of

things. I think it is only right I should protest very emphatically against the bringing down of Supplementary Estimates aggregating $36,723,120.66 within the last days of a long and wearisome session when the heat is so great that it is only with the greatest moral courage and devotion to the public interest that members si 1 late at night for the purpose of considering them.
Public Works - London - public building, $400,000.

Besides this vote in these Supplementary Estimates there were in the Main Estimates a number of large appropriations for public buildings in other places, involving large amounts of money. This matter of public buildings is one which concerns a great many constituteneies, and I dare say the position of many members is similar to my own. My constituents are constantly putting forward representations that the public business requires larger buildings and better accommodation generally. At the request of the Ministers of the Crown I have pointed out to them that this is not a time for spending money on public buildings if the expenditure can possibly be deferred. Nevertheless, I see in the Estimates votes for a number of public buildings in different parts of the country, and unless there is some special reason why these appropriations should be voted I wish to protest on behalf of other members as well as myself who have been advising their constituents that money for these purposes was not available, and that they should wait until normal times return before asking the Government to go ahead with large expenditures. Perhaps the minister can tell us whether there1 are any special reasons why votes of this magnitude should now be brought down unexpectedly. I must confess I find it very difficult indeed, to reconcile these expenditures with the explanation I have given to my constituents. I cannot see why London, Ontario, which is getting a public building costing $400,000, should be placed, on a different footing from Truro, Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I wish I had time to discuss this matter a little more fully. There is a great deal in what the hon. gentleman states, but he will remember that in the early days of this session I stated what the policy of the Government was to be regarding public buildings, and in the Main Estimates provision was made only for a public building at Montreal-a vote of $500,000, which, of course, will not complete the building-one in Toronto, one in

Hamilton, and one in Calgary. I think those are all the new public buildings provided for in the Main Estimates. I know that my hon. friend feels he is entitled to a public building in Truro. I know a vote was put in the Estimates a few years ago for a public building there, and a site was purchased. I know where it is, because I am well acquainted with the town of Truro, and I am not saving that a public building there is not a necessity.
What is true of Truro would be true of a hundred other towns in Canada. I believe we had applications for at least a hundred public buildings and in very many of these places some twenty-five sites have been purchased. There were so many that it became a question of policy. I am always willing to take a full share, of responsibility, but personally I was opposed to going on with these public buildings except where they were absolutely necessary and would provide employment, which is an important considerar tion at 'the present time. This matter was not decided by the Public Works Departr ment, although I state frankly what my position was. It was decided by Council as a whole and whatever has been done, my friends can be assured, is a well settled question of policy decided by the Government. In trying to carry out that policy I had to depart from it only in two cases, where I felt it was necessary. The city of London has a building that is very antiquated, entirely inadequate for the services, and we are paying a large amount in rentals. I went there personally and looked it over and was thoroughly satisfied that they are very much hampered. As a matter of policy, therefore, we are asking Parliament to vote $400,000 in connection with this building. The other case is in Kamloops, where they have an old wooden post office that has been there for a great many years. The town has grown away from it, and I came to the conclusion, after careful consideration, that a building was a necessity. We are putting in the Estimates only $20,000 for Kamloops, which will put us in a position 'to make a .start. I am fairly positive that those are the only two instances in which the principle has been departed from in the Supplementary Estimates You will see a number of cases of repairs and extensions. There are some repairs to the Brandon public building, Portage la Prairie public building, and one or two places in Ontario, I have forgotten where.
They have been in the Main Estimates for the last three or four years.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
If so we shall certainly go ahead. We are going ahead with everything in the Main Estimates as rapidly as we can. There is no branch of the Public Works Department that has been so much rushed for the last two years as the architectural branch. This has been so especially during the last year, for we have had the duty of constructing military hospitals, military buildings, etc. Everything is being rushed as speedily as possible, and the hon. gentleman can rest assured that in connection with any buildings for which votes have been granted the work will be proceeded. with at the earliest possible moment.
Mr. MoCURDY: I must congratulate the hon. member for London (Mr. Cronyn) on his success. The business for which the building at Truro to which I alluded is to be used is important. The Department of Public Works recognized years ago that it was necessary, and acquired a site at a time when the revenues received at that office were less than half of what they are to-day.
I make the plea for that building that in my opinion it is not reasonable or fair that the smaller centres of population should be neglected while larger expenditures are made in connection with buildings in large cities.

The minister well said in reference to accommodations in London that the building in existence: there to-day is a very old one. It was built some sixty-four years ago and has served its purpose well. The idea of putting up a public building to meet the requirements of that section today is not something that has. sprung up at this session. It was conceded as a necessity by the Government many years ago, and in 1912 the Government purchased a property adjoining the post office there at a cost of $145,000. That is an ancient building, built about the same time as the post office. The revenue and business in the London office is entirely out of proportion to a population of 60,000. London is the hub and centre of a population of considerably more than a million people, and London and that district has completely outgrown this building. At present the different departments, customs and post office, have to be housed entirely outside the building. London is also now the centre of the taxation department of the Government for that district and it requires a considerable staff, and the pressure to have this building is not only from the member interested,, but from the departments of the Government, to provide adecpicite accoimno-

dation for their needs. It is important in the interests of the service, I think, that the building should be proceeded with.

I want to impress upon the Minister of Public Works the urgent necessity of proceeding with needed public buildings in the Maritime Provinces. I do so, however, not by criticising the Minister of Public Works, who has endeavoured to convey the idea to us that his hand's are tied by the Government in regard to the expenditures for this purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will pardon me, but I did not intend to convey any such idea to the Committee. On the contrary I stated that I entirely agreed with the policy which has been adopted.

Then the minister's hands are tied willingly, and that is the reason why there are such few places that are to get public buildings during the present year. If the Government had followed that policy in other matters, I would not be so critical about it, but in a very great many cases the floodt'gates of extravagance have been opened wide and money has been poured out throughout this country for purposes that will not come within nearly measurable distances' of being .so useful, or being so. greatly in the interests of the people, as will the erection of public buildings. My hon. friend (Mr. Glass) stated that the post office in London had1 ,been built for sixty-four years. In my town the post office is 164 years old, judging by the looks of it.
It can be preserved as an antique.

It can be preserved as an antique; nevertheless the town is just as much entitled to a decent post office where our people can get their mail matter under comfortable circumstances, as is the city of Montreal. The necessity that exists for proper accommodation is just as urgent in Saokville as it is in any oither city. The same thing can he said in regard to giving employment to returned soldiers. The argument is advanced that only in the large cities does the necessity exist for providing returned soldiers with employment. The need is just as great to give work to 
these men in the smaller towns as it is in the larger cities. In the town of Sackville, where I reside, the post office is of such diminutive character that not one-tenth of those who go for their mail of a winter's evening can get inside the building; they have to wait in uncomfortable surroundings. Now the Government can find as large a sum as $250,000 to increase the salaries of the judges of the Dominion, make them comfortable and, as was said by the hon. gentleman who was fathering the Bill the other night, provide them with the necessaries of life. Again the Government finds it easy to appropriate $1,000 a year to augment the salary of each of a number of highly paid officials throughout the Civil Service. Yet the people of the Maritime Provinces cannot be decently served with postal facilities or with proper accommodation when they go for their mails. I put myself on record as being absolutely opposed to such a system as that. If economies in the public expenditures are to be made, let them apply equally in all sections of the country, and let us all undergo the sacrifices which are necessary to an equal extent. A great deal has been said in this House about this being a war year and that consequently we must keep our expenditures down to a very low figure. But why practice economy in a few instances in certain sections of Canada and then resort to such extravagance in other parts as the Government has done during the past year? I take my stand along with my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. McCurdy) and protest against such a policy on the part of the Government. The Maritime Provinces have never been given decent or reasonable treatment in this, or other matters, by the present or past governments. They have not been properly treated, and the time has come when, unless the representatives of the provinces in this Parliament assert their rights, and make a claim for what is due, we shall have no chance of maintaining our public buildings as they have been maintained in the other towns and cities throughout the Dominion. The same criticism must be made in respect to railway accommodation in the Maritime Provinces. During the past year or two the Intercolonial has been starved toy the Minister of Railways. Rolling stock has been taken from that system and placed on other railways, and yet when we ask for needed expenditures we are told this is a war year and nothing can be done. The Government is expending millions of dollars else-

where, and then we are told we cannot even have a small public building. They have provided proper facilities in Montreal, in Toronto, in Winnipeg, and elsewhere in the West-in fact, they have been generous everywhere else except in the Maritime Provinces. I want to declare myself as being absolutely opposed to any such policy as that. If sacrifices are to be made and economies are to be practised, let them apply everywhere to the country generally, to one part as well as to another. No good reason has been given to this Committee why certain portions of the Dominion have to be starved in the matter of public expenditures, while other parts of the country are "fed up" and public moneys expended so lavishly as they have been durin-g the past year by the Government.

I think I should ask the minister for some information in respect to conditions in my own county with respect to the Inverness railway. He is aware that I have been discussing this matter with him and the Government for sometime past, and that I showed the Government we are in a pretty serious difficulty down there with respect to the only railway we have-the Inverness railway. The minister is no doubt aware that tha,t railway is to be closed down soon, and that the Inverness coal mine is also to cease operating about the 10th of this month. I have endeavoured for some time past to impress upon the Government the importance of taking over this road as a branch to the Government roads. I think it is clear to the minister and to the Committee that branch lines, as such, have not been successful as business enterprises, particularly in our part of the country. This branch line, I think, has merits perhaps superior to those of any branch line in Eastern Canada, as was shown the Government from time to time, particularly for the past six months. But it has had a very unfortunate history. I am not going to discuss the merits of this road from the standpoint of prospective earnings. I have already placed in the hands of the minister and the Government all the facts in connection with it. I have advised him that the natural resources of West Cape Breton island are superior in variety and value to those of any other section in the Maritime Provinces, or possibly in the Dominion, according to its size. If this road closes down the only coal industry we have will of necessity close down also, and general paralysis of our industrial life will follow. If the Government takes over the road as a branch of the Intercolonial, I can tell the

Committee it will prove to be the best earning line of its length in Canada, as I have already shown the Government on more than one occasion.
I will not at this time undertake to give the House a full account of the resources of the country served by this line. It would require more time than can be spared at this late hour, in view of the fact that I have already put all this information in the hands of the Government. What are the views of the minister with regard to the taking over of this line and its operation as a branch of the Intercolonial? The matter is all-important to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I made up my mind a year or two ago that we should take over the branch lines in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and get rid of all the troubles the people were having because of these lines not ''being properly operated. Last year we were able to make arrangements with several of the railways in New Brunswick, although two of them would not accept the offer that we made and, consequently, have not yet been taken over. We have been urged to take over two or three in Nova Scotia, one of them in Richmond county and one in Inverness. I have tried to avoid doing anything at the present time, but I am informed that the Inverness road will be closed down if something is not done.
I have been prepared, therefore, to recommend that we take over that road on the same basis as that upon which the roads in Nova Scotia have been taken over. They value the road at $150,000, the equipment, including 7 engines, and 131 coal cars, at $175,000, and supplies at $25,000; and they offered to sell the road, equipment, and supplies at those figures. I replied that I would submit the matter to Council on the basis *of paying $150,000 for the road and, for the equipment and such supplies as should be taken over, a sum to be determined upon a valuation made by Mr. Hanna. If it were not so late in the session, in the event of a decision to take the road over, we could have placed an amount in the Estimates for that purpose and explained'the matter more fully to Parliament. The only way in which we can act before the 10th of this month is under the Branch Lines Act, and if this should be done the agreement would be laid before the House at the next session. I am glad the hon. member has brought the matter up, because I would not want the House to think that an arrangement of this kind had been made with this or any other railroad only a day or
two after the prorogation of Parliament. I shall, therefore, submit the matter to Council, and if Council agrees, to the proposal on approximately the basis that has been suggested, it is altogether likely that the road will be taken over by the Government and will therefore not cease operation. In the meantime, in order that the road may not close down during the first ten days of July, I understand, orders have been given for 1,800 tons of coal a week for that road in order to keep it in operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I should think the hon. member must know that there is no interference in any way, shape or form by the Department of Railways or by the Government. The management are operating the railways free from any interference by any member of the Government and I believe, from any member of Parliament. The only thing that I	said	to _ Mr. .Hanna was this, that the policy of the Government	was	to give
returned soldiers positions first; that they must have the preference whenever any man was required, and after that, of course, the management would have to select employees from those available. I have had no complaints in regard to the matter, and I should like to know it, if it can be shown that any political patronage is being exercised. Officials may be doing it of their own accord, but it has not been brought to my attention.

My hon. friend has been telling me ever since I became a member of the House that there was not patronage on the Intercolonial. I have told him differently, but of course he is not obliged to take my word. More than that I have placed affidavits on Hansard showing that there was patronage on the Intercolonial. Even if the minister doubted my word he should give some consideration to sworn affidavits. We have also heard a great deal about what the Government is doing for the returned soldiers, how they are to be given preference in appointments to the Government service. I yield to no one in my admiration for the returned soldier, and I think it is only right that returned soldiers should be given the preference where they are capable of filling the position. But I have heard very often that as a matter of fact the returned soldiers are not given the preference in different departments of the public service. I have heard, for instance, that they have not been given the preference on the Canadian National Railways. Complaints have been made to me that returned soldiers who have applied for vacant positions on the Canadian National Railways have been turned down. I have some definite information on this point. Recently
I received a letter from one authorized to speak for the returned soldiers, I would think, to the effect that they are not getting the consideration they deserve and which the Government promised. I have a letter heTe from the Employment and Service Branch of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-Establishment, Moncton, which reads as follows:
Embodied in this letter you will find a few plain facts of what the returned soldier is UP against in this city and in the eastern .provinces.
In the first place if he goes to the C.N.R. General Offices to apply for a position he is given to understand by the Chief Clerk or some petty official that it is an impossibility for him to see Mr. L. S. Brown, and if! by chance he happens to see Mr. Brown, this gentleman informs him that he is willing to put him to work, but that there are no vacancies, at the present time, and he will have to wait his turn.
All during the war the Government was held up for men in the mechanical departments in the shops, so that they took on any one who applied to them, wn0 was not eligible tor soldiering. In several oases they were men from the United States who came under the Military 'Service Act in their own oountry but by coming to Canada they did not come under the Canadian Act. They went to work in the Government works and are still holding their positions.
These facts are very well founded, and I would like to have them taken up at the next session of the House to see if steps cannot be taken to break down the barrier on the Government works here, and make vacancies for returned men hy dismissing war workers.
This is not the opinion of a dissatisfied soldier. This is voiced hy every returned man in the district, and seems to be the talk of the town, and is taken up at all public meetings.
The letter is signed by the representative of the D.S.C.R., Moncton. Apparently he is a returned soldier employed by the Government to assist other returned soldiers in getting work. I do not want to make his name public, but I shall be very glad to give it to the minister so that he may make inquiries. I would imagine that this man is in charge of an employment bureau in the city of Moncton for returned soldiers. And what does he say? That when a soldier goes to see the officials of the railway these high-salaried gentlemen will not see him. Some petty official is placed outside the door who tells him it is impossible for him to get an interview. Is that the way the soldiers were used when they were called upon to enlist? Is that the way they were treated when the Conscription Act came into force? It is certainly not the way they were told they would be used when they went overseas; it is certainly not the way they were told they would be used when they got back home to Canada. I repeat, this information comes from

speechtext: I would like to pass all these items, except one, on which a general discussion can be had.
That will be all right.
I have some observations to make on the Hudson Bay railway.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
can discuss the matter on item 96, which is a vote of $35,000,000 for miscellaneous railway equipment. That is the object in having that item stand.
Will the item be taken up in the morning?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: There are two Bills to be dealt with and then we will go on to Estimates.
The trouble is that we never know when the Estimates come up.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Generally notice is
given the night before of the programme for the following day.

I did not understand
there was any possibility of the Railway Estimates coming up to-night, but some of us stayed around and that is how we come to be present now.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I did not expect the
Railway Estimates would be taken up until a short time ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Then item No. 96
stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, and any matter
affecting our railways can be discussed in connection with it.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Reid the House adjourned at 2.30 a.m., Saturday.
Saturday, July 5, 1919.
